title: When could Spotify Wrapped 2024 come out?
body:
A year tracking your musical highs and lows is soon upon us

Were you to tap or scroll through your array of social media accounts on a certain day in early December, you will be sure to almost exclusively see a deluge of Spotify screenshots.

Famously started by a plucky intern in 2015, what is now an annual event was re-branded from a “Year in Music” to “Spotify Wrapped” in 2015.

Each year, Spotify users’ top artists, songs and podcasts are shared in eye-catching, succinct animations ready to be shared with the masses.

Listeners are also presented with a playlist of their top 100 songs of the year.

Now, somewhat of an event in the festive calendar, come autumn, murmurs of people’s year of listening being available for all to see begin to arise.

Here is everything you need to know about Spotfy’s biggest day of the year.

An official date for Spotify Wrapped’s release is yet to be announced, but it is expected in early December.

The streaming platform typically announces its wrapped date through its social media channels, and the same is expected this year.

Spotify Wrapped is perhaps one of the most successful examples of “user-generated marketing”, marketing that relies on, mostly social media users, reposting and distributing material.

When the time comes, the process should be simple, when you enter the Spotify app it should just be on your homepage.

It is unknown between which periods Spotify begins and finishes logging your listening data.

However, Spotify told its users on 24 October that “2024 is almost a wrap,” telling listeners to “get wrapped-ready”.

Due to many people being somewhat ashamed of their guilty pleasure tunes being broadcast to their friends, many are keen to know when their window of opportunity for low-brow listening opens.

Reporting from Billboard and others a few years back is what led to people believing that Spotify only takes your listening habits up until 31 October into account when creating Wrapped, but it turns out that that is not so.

Responding to a tweet from Pop Crave about Wrapped ending on Halloween in 2022, the official Spotify account said: “The only thing that we end on Halloween is eating candy corn. Stream (and snack) all through the year and we will see you in Wrapped season.”

Spotify’s vice president of product development, Babar Zafar, shed a little more light on the process before 2023’s Wrapped: “The Wrapped personalised experience covers streaming for 2022, so beginning in January and ending a few weeks prior to the launch on 30 November,” he said.

“We aim to leave the cut-off date as late as possible to really create a truly personalised experience for the millions of listeners around the world.”
topics: Explainer, Spotify

title: National insurance hike will hit 'essential' charity services, Reeves warned
body:
Charities have called for themselves to be made exempt from any rise in NI in Wednesday's Budget

Charities are warning they may be forced to reduce their services if Rachel Reeves goes ahead with plans to increase national insurance (NI) on employers at the Budget this week.

The Chancellor is expected to announce an increase to employer NI contributions in Wednesday’s Budget, but there have been calls for the third sector to be exempt from any extra taxes.

Although public sector organisations are set to receive additional funding to cover the extra costs, the private sector and voluntary sector are expected to have to use their own funds to meet the additional burden, with warnings that smaller charities in particular would find the change difficult.

Matthew Reed, the chief executive of palliative care charity Marie Curie, told i that it would need to find new sources of income or face having to scale back its services.

He said: “Increasing the national insurance on a charity already dependent on donations from the public will have a detrimental impact on the amount of care we are able to provide.

“We will now need to ask for more funding from our NHS partners or rely further on kind donations from the public to continue to provide our services.”

Reeves has warned of a £22bn “black hole” in the nation’s finances which needs to be filled, and is said to be looking at raising £40bn in total from cuts and tax rises.

She is boxed in, however, by manifesto commitments not to raise income tax, national insurance on workers, or VAT. It is widely expected she will raise amount of national insurance employers pay by 1 or 2 per cent and cut the earnings threshold at which the tax is paid.

These moves together could raise £20bn and allow the Government to argue it has honoured its commitment not to raise taxes on working people.

The National Council for Voluntary Organisations (NCVO) – the membership organisation for the charity sector – warned however that the extra tax will add pressure on to charities, and may force them to “divert” funds away from essential services.

Sarah Elliott, the organisation’s CEO, told i: “An increase in employer NI contributions would add another financial strain on charities already facing rising service costs, reduced income, and surging demand. The pressure from this tax rise will be felt across the sector but will be especially challenging for smaller charities to manage.

“With over half of sector employees working in organisations with fewer than 50 staff, small charities are at the heart of our communities, providing a crucial safety net where public services fall short.

“Increasing employer contributions could force these charities to divert already stretched finances away from essential services, or even reduce their support altogether – putting the communities they support at risk.”

The NCV) – along with the Scottish Council for Voluntary Organisations, Northern Ireland Council for Voluntary Action and Wales Council for Voluntary Actio -, have written to the Chancellor calling for charities to get the same treatment as the public sector, which is set to be exempt from the extra tax.

“With costs climbing, funding falling, and demand for services increasing, our sector already faces a crisis. The additional costs placed on the sector by increasing employers’ national insurance contributions will only compound this,” the letter states.

“As you navigate the significant financial challenges the country faces, we are confident that it would not be your intention to place them at the door of charities and community organisations. We are not asking for special treatment, just parity with the public sector.”

Mr Reed said that governments have a “history of not properly considering non-NHS providers of NHS services” – such as Marie Curie – when making fiscal decisions.

“We need to see non-NHS providers of NHS services fully funded especially given these national insurance increases,” he added.

“We urgently need the Government to recognise that there needs to be a sustainable funding model for palliative and end-of-life care. We need a co-ordinated, joined-up approach, so that dying people, and their loved ones get the support they need, where they want to be, whatever their illness.”

Jo Walby, CEO of Manchester-based charity Mustard Tree, which works to prevent homelessness, said charities should be exempt from any increase in employer NI.

She told i: “The past few years have been tough for everyone, and we know that the Government will make some tough decisions, but adding real cost to a charity like Mustard Tree directly impacts our ability to cope with the increase in demand that we are seeing.

“We have reduced our costs as much as we can this year to free up some cash so that we can add support workers to our team to help people out of poverty and homelessness. This increase in NI would wipe out those cost savings and means our existing staff and volunteers must do even more to try and cope with the increasing numbers through our doors, without the resources they need.

“Charities should be exempt from the change.”

Jo Henney, CEO at Nugent – a social care charity in Liverpool – told i: “The social care sector is already stretched to its limits with underpaid and undervalued staff and although the new government is keen not to affect working people, increasing the taxes for employers will surely do that as budgets and workforces are forced to shrink.

“At Nugent, we pride ourselves on being a Real Living Wage employer – our colleagues are among the most skilled and dedicated workforce in the country and we want to reward them accordingly – but this will see us pay more tax.

“Our main outlets to pass these costs on to are charges to the local authorities, which are already our main source of income and don’t have additional funds to support, or restricting pay rises to colleagues who work hard all year round. Less money will also be available for core missions and initiatives within charities and could affect the essential services that charities provide – making ‘need to haves’ into ‘nice to haves’.”

Businesses have also warned that an increase to their tax burden could end up having an impact on employees, either through lower wages or less hiring.

Craig Beaumont, executive director at the Federation of Small Businesses, previously told i that an increase in employer NI would “make every job in all our local communities more expensive to maintain”.

He added: “Fewer jobs and lower pay is not the way forward.”
topics: Budget, Money, Rachel Reeves

title: If your payslip could be hit by the Budget and when changes will take effect
body:
Ministers have denied that workers will see changes on their payslips, but experts disagree

Labour has promised that tax rises announced at Wednesday’s Budget will not hit workers’ payslips.

On Sunday, Education Secretary Bridget Phillipson said workers will not see higher taxes “on their payslip”, as ministers battle to explain what was meant by their manifesto pledge not to increase taxes on “working people”.

But financial experts have told i they do not think the interpretation is correct, and that some may see an impact on their take-home pay in the future.

Below, we run through some of the potential changes in this week’s Budget, and when they could have an impact on your payslip.

Presented by the Chancellor, the Budget will reportedly make tax rises and spending cuts worth £40bn.

But in the party’s manifesto for the general election, Labour promised that it would not increase VAT, national insurance (NI) or income tax on working people.

Phillipson told BBC One’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: “And coming out of this Budget, working people will not see higher taxes on the payslips that they receive.

“That is really important, because we know the pressures that people are under,” she said.

But experts have told i otherwise, with Tracy Crookes, financial planner at Quilter, saying that “people will ultimately feel the tax burden rise without anything changing”.

Rachel Reeves is widely expected to announce a further freeze to tax thresholds on Wednesday.

Thresholds typically increase in line with inflation to account for rising wages but have not done so since 2021, meaning in real-terms people pay more tax, because they generally have higher salaries than they did in 2021.

People start paying the basic rate of income tax, as well as national insurance, once they earn £12,570 – a threshold known as the personal allowance.

The freeze is set to end in 2028, but Labour is poised to extend this to 2030. This means that the Labour decision would hit pay packets from 2028 onwards.

Tracy Crookes said: “As wages grow in line with inflation, state tax thresholds will drag more and more individuals into higher tax brackets, a phenomenon known as fiscal drag.

“For millions of middle-income earners, this means paying a higher proportion of their income in tax without seeing any real increase in their purchasing power.”

“The fact that this policy allows the Government to increase tax revenue without officially ‘raising taxes’ is little more than semantics. It is a stealth tax that, over time, could undermine trust in the Government’s promises”.

Income tax thresholds are expected to be frozen for a year or more beyond the current end date of 2028.

Sarah Coles, head of personal finance at Hargreaves Lansdown, said this would cost people billions of their earnings as the Government takes a bigger slice of any pay rises.

She said: “Frozen thresholds will kick in when the current freeze expires in 2028.”

An employer has to pay 13.8 per cent national insurance (NI) on an employee’s salary, but there are suggestions this could be increased at the Budget.

Even though this would be a tax levied on businesses, rather than individuals, experts suggest that the increases could eventually filter through to employees, perhaps in the form of lower wages.

Craig Rickman, personal finance expert at interactive investor told i: “If businesses pay more tax, they could look to make cuts elsewhere to balance things out.

“This could mean lower future pay rises, smaller bonuses, and less generous pension contributions for staff.”

Businesses of all sizes would be impacted by this change, he said, from large businesses with vast structures and lots of employees to small-to-medium-sized private limited companies, who either draw a reasonable director’s salary and/or employ a few staff.

These could start filtering through after the tax changes take effect.

Changes in Budgets often start in the new tax year, which would be 6 April 2025, Mr Morrow McDade said.

However, he added: “There is a precedent for mid-year changes in NI contributions as Rishi Sunak did in January of this year. I suspect a change might come into force in January 2025 to give time for updates to the payroll systems.”
topics: Budget, Labour, Rachel Reeves, Tax

title: I survived cancer - Amy Dowden is showing us the scary reality of remission
body:
After the Strictly dancer's collapse backstage, Rosamund Dean tells how she underestimated the challenges of life after treatment

Seeing Amy Dowden back on Strictly Come Dancing this year has filled me – and more than six million other viewers – with so much joy.

The 34-year-old dancer, one of the stars of the BBC’s Saturday night juggernaut, has become a national sweetheart after the way in which she handled being diagnosed with breast cancer last spring.

Amy has undergone brutal treatment over the past year, including chemotherapy and mastectomy surgery, and has chosen to be completely honest and vulnerable about the realities of treatment on Instagram, where she has almost 700,000 followers.

So it was upsetting to hear that she was treated in hospital after collapsing backstage during Saturday’s live Halloween special. Amy and her partner, JB Gill of boy band JLS, had just performed the foxtrot to Toploader’s “Dancing In The Moonlight” when she became unwell. A spokesperson has said that an ambulance was called “as a precaution” and she is already “feeling much better.” However, it has since been reported that professional dancer Lauren Oakley will step in to temporarily replace Amy as JB’s partner, while she makes a full recovery.

Of course, this illness may have nothing to do with breast cancer – Amy also has Crohn’s disease, which can cause debilitating pain and fatigue. But anyone who has been through cancer treatment (and one in seven British women will receive a breast cancer diagnosis in their lifetime) knows that life after treatment can be scary and unpredictable.

I became one of those statistics after being diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021, aged 40. Thanks to 18 months of gruelling chemotherapy, mastectomy surgery, radiotherapy, and then further adjuvant chemo for good measure, I am now in remission. But I completely underestimated how difficult post-cancer life could be.

Chemotherapy caused my body to go into overnight menopause. This meant that the chemo side effects of fatigue, insomnia, brain fog and mood swings didn’t lift when treatment ended, since many of these are also menopausal symptoms. Not only that, but I now had early-onset osteoporosis in my spine, thanks to chemo and early menopause. Post-surgical complications included lymphoedema in my right hand (swelling caused by removing underarm lymph nodes, where they had also found cancer cells).

Besides the ongoing physical impact of treatment, I was also dealing with the psychological effects. Battered and scarred by treatment, my nervous system was on high alert, hyper-vigilant for signs of recurrence.

Just as my friends and family were expecting me to be happy and relieved, I was feeling worse than ever. People think that, when active treatment is over and the cancer is gone, then you can get “back to normal”. But, like many women, I learned that it’s unfortunately not so simple.

Earlier this year, I interviewed Amy about her experience of coping with ongoing issues such as early menopause (which she also experienced) after treatment.

“In a way, it might help that I’m a dancer, because I understand my body quite well,” she said. “And also because I’ve had Crohn’s disease since the age of 11, so I’m quite symptom and body-aware from that.”

She touched on something that is so important: learning to get back in tune with your body after treatment. So many women find that, after months of being jabbed with needles and pumped full of toxic drugs, they have disassociated from their own body. Many women find that a physical activity – whether dance, yoga or something else – can help them feel a bit more like themselves again.

As well as reconnecting with your body after treatment, another thing I’ve learnt is that it’s so important to be open about how you feel emotionally. It can actually be really difficult to let those close to you know that you’re struggling. There is a sense of not wanting to let loved-ones down, particularly when they are so keen to see you feeling better – but this can make the fear and anxiety worse because it’s being bottled up inside.

I found that the anxiety lifted when I was able to talk about it; first with a therapist, and then being able to explain to those closest to me that recovery is not a linear process. Some days I’ll be feeling energetic, optimistic and almost back to my old self. On other days, it’s much more of a struggle.

The same goes for returning to work after treatment. Putting on a brave face might feel like the only option in some situations, but most bosses and workplaces will be understanding that the after-effects of treatment might mean it will take time before you can be firing on all cylinders at work again. Some women even find that a breast cancer diagnosis makes them completely reevaluate their life, including their work, and leave their job or have a career change.

In Amy’s case, Strictly is her dream job, and always has been. So it’s great to see that BBC bosses are being sympathetic and accommodating about the fact that her health must come first. I know the rest of the nation is with me in hoping to see her back on the dance floor very soon.

Rosamund Dean is the author of Reconstruction: How to Rebuild Your Body, Mind and Life After a Breast Cancer Diagnosis
topics: Breast Cancer, Cancer, Features, Lifestyle, Strictly Come Dancing, Subscribers, Wellbeing

title: Why non-EU tourists could soon pay more at French attractions
body:
The mayor of Paris has said the idea of making religious people pay to worship at the Notre Dame is 'morally shocking'

British travellers could face another Brexit penalty if a plan backed by the French culture minister, Rachida Dati, goes ahead.

Non-EU citizens may soon have to pay extra to visit popular tourist attractions, as Ms Dati says such a move is necessary to “finance the renovation of the national heritage”.

Visitors who don’t hold an EU passport could be charged an extra €5 (around £4.17) to enter the Louvre in Paris, where the levy is set to be implemented first.

The standard adult entry price for the art museum is €22 (€18.30), which would increase to €27 for Britons under Ms Dati’s plan. Visitors who are under 18 and people aged 18-25 who are residents of the European Economic Area (the EU, Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein) can enter for free.

If the price rise for non-EU visitors does come into force at the Louvre, attractions such as the Palace of Versailles and the Musée D’Orsay could soon follow suit.

Ms Dati is also said to be considering an entry fee for Notre Dame Cathedral, which is set to reopen in December following 2019’s fire. If that goes ahead, it would be the first time in the building’s history that entry would not be free to all.

The Mayor of Paris Centre, Ariel Weil, immediately pushed back on her proposal, saying the idea of making religious people pay to worship is “morally shocking”.

It’s not yet clear whether or not the fee would apply to those who choose to pray at Notre Dame, however.

Regardless, Ms Dati told Le Figaro that her “position is very clear”.

“I want visitors from outside the EU to pay more for their entrance ticket and for this supplement to finance the renovation of the national heritage.”

“The French people should not have to pay for everything on their own.”

While her plans do seem to include all non-EU citizens, some have suggested that it’s a particular attack on British people. UK citizens visit France more than any other nation, making up some 14.8 per cent of visitors there annually.

In response, UK culture minister Chris Bryant posted on X criticising the plan and reiterating that entry to the UK’s national galleries and museums is “Free to all. You’re welcome”.

While Ms Dati’s proposal is controversial, it isn’t particularly unusual in many tourist hot spots around the world.

In Istanbul, foreign visitors to the Basilica Cistern pay four times as much as Turkish tourists. Other attractions in the city also have two-tier payment systems.

The Hagia Sophia Grand Mosque recently introduced a fee of 850 Turkish Lira (£19) for all foreign visitors as well as Turkish non-Muslims.

Elsewhere in Europe, some restaurateurs are allegedly being less up-front about their different charges for locals and tourists.

In Lisbon, the Expresso newspaper has suggested that some restaurants should give menus with higher prices to customers who don’t speak Portuguese.

Expresso’s report also claims that the lower prices for Portuguese speakers can be “transmitted verbally, in whispers or indicated on menus placed in inconspicuous or even hidden areas”.

Portugal’s AHRESP hospitality industry association has said it’s not aware of such practices.

Up the coast, Portugal‘s second city of Porto last month confirmed it will double its daily tourist charge in order to help fund its culture and heritage as well as practical aspects of daily life. Porto is following in the footsteps of the capital Lisbon, which has recently implemented the same tax increase for tourists.

And it’s not just Portugal.

Last week, authorities in Venice announced that this year’s pilot scheme to crack down on overtourism in the Italian city has worked well and will be extended.

In 2025, they will almost double the number of days – to 59 – on which day trippers will be charged €5 (€4.17) to enter.

Political leaders there bemoan the fact that these visitors, who tend to spend just a few hours in Venice, clog up its streets and attractions but add little to the economy.

Greece is taking a similar approach.

Its government has decided to charge cruise passengers visiting Santorini and Mykonos €20 (€16.60).

Both islands attract millions of foreign visitors every year, with Santorini alone receiving 1.3 million cruise passengers in 2023.

Authorities say the only option is to charge tourists who only visit briefly a high amount in order to combat increased traffic, busy streets and environmental damage.

In India, the Taj Mahal has long charged foreign visitors significantly more for entry than its own citizens. Overseas visitors pay the equivalent of £15 to visit, a far steeper figure than the £2.20 charged to residents.

In Tokyo, a two-tier payment system for residents and visitors is commonplace in restaurants.

There, overtourism and the struggling currency has seen a number of restaurants charging different prices for foreigners, although owners claim they’re not charging tourists more, rather their food costs less for locals.

This year, Japan is set to attract a record number of tourists. In response, places country-wide have been implementing tourist taxes.

Tourism authorities in Hokkaido have urged businesses to set lower prices for locals and the mayor responsible for the Unesco-listed Himeji Castle in the west has announced that he’s considering charging foreign tourists more than six times the local entry rate.

Further south in Asia, other countries are already implementing these stringent measures.

Thailand has a two-tier cost policy across its entire national park network.

Across the country, international visitors have to fork out five times the amount its citizens do, regardless of the size or popularity of the park they’re visiting.

Over the border in Cambodia, entrance to the Angkor Wat temple complex is free for citizens but costs the equivalent of £29 for a day’s entry for tourists from elsewhere.

More than two million foreign visitors opt to pay that fee every year.
topics: Brexit Travel, Europe Travel, France, France Travel, Overtourism, Paris

title: I'm dying from lung disease at 48 after working on kitchen revamps
body:
Marek Marzec has terminal silicosis after inhaling toxic dust while cutting engineered stone worktops

A stonemason with only weeks to live after contracting a deadly lung disease from cutting kitchen worktops for home revamps said he wants to warn of the dangers before he dies.

Marek Marzec, 48, is receiving end-of-life care in a London hospital after being diagnosed with silicosis in April this year.

The father-of-three from Poland is among a growing number of tradesmen diagnosed with the incurable disease after inhaling toxic dust while cutting quartz engineered – or artificial – stone worktops, which have soared in popularity among homeowners in recent years.

Mr Marzec, who spent 12 years in London and Hertfordshire cutting engineered stone slabs, described working in appalling conditions, surrounded by dust “like a tornado” so thick he couldn’t see more than a yard.

Speaking from his hospital bed, he said employers failed to provide adequate safety equipment, and when he asked for a dust extraction tool at one firm, he was told that he could leave if he wasn’t happy.

“They [the doctors] say I am on my way to death, but when it’s happening, no one can tell,” he told i from his bed in Whittington Hospital.

“There was a chance I could get a lung transplant, but now I hear that this option is really out. It’s a very difficult situation. I would give anything to continue on living.”

He arrived in the UK in 2011, hoping to build a better life and wanting to make sure his young daughters were financially secure.

“Instead, because of the work I did cutting quartz worktops, I have been left unable to breathe and in terrible pain,” he said.

“I cannot tell you how angry I am that I was allowed to work in these conditions and that my life has been cut short simply for doing my job.

“I am not the only person whose life has been put at risk by this lethal dust. It is time for urgent action to stop these dangerous working conditions I had to face before other stone workers contract this terrible disease and die.”

In February, i revealed that the first cases of silicosis had been diagnosed in engineered stone tradesmen in the UK, most of them young migrants working in poor conditions, echoing a trend seen in other countries. All of them are men.

i previously reported that confirmed cases in the UK have doubled in recent months, with 16 men now diagnosed, the youngest aged 24. One has died and two have been referred for lung transplant assessment.

A doctors’ report in August into the first eight cases, led by occupational lung disease consultant Dr Jo Feary from the Royal Brompton, found their average age was 34, and warned the numbers are set to rise significantly in coming years.

The doctors urged the Government to consider a ban on the stone.

Quartz worktops have become an increasingly popular choice for kitchen refurbishments, but the manmade stone contains high amounts of silica.

When the material is cut and large amounts of its dust inhaled, it can cause silicosis, an incurable lung disease that has afflicted workers in industries like mining or construction for decades.

Tradesmen cutting and polishing the countertops before installation have reported a lack of water suppression to dampen dust through ‘wet’ cutting in small workshops and inappropriate respiratory protection.

In July, Australia became the first country in the world to ban engineered stone after hundreds of stonemasons were diagnosed with silicosis, most aged under 35, according to a report by policy body Safe Work Australia.

Almost 200 cases have occurred in California since 2019, the majority being Latino migrants, of whom 13 died. There are also outbreaks in other countries, including Spain and Israel.

Mr Marzec and his lawyers at Leigh Day have now launched legal action against three companies he was employed by, where he alleges he was exposed to unsafe conditions that are likely to have led to his diagnosis.

“We just had masks, and there was no extractor at all. [The dust] was really like when you are in a tornado. You wouldn’t see anything a yard away from you,” he said.

“I asked my employer for an extractor, but he said no, and if you’re unhappy about no extractor here, you can just leave. But it’s not that simple. I have young kids to support.

“I know from a friend that in his workshop there was just one small machine, and in the workshop that I used to work in, the ceiling was just almost above me, while it really needs to be high up – at least three metres.

“So the whole room was really too small for this kind of work.”

While on holiday a year ago, he noticed he had symptoms when he went swimming and found he couldn’t cover the same distance as he usually would.

His breathing became more laboured, and on 20 April this year he was diagnosed with acute silicosis. He deteriorated rapidly and his condition is now terminal, with doctors telling him he has weeks to live.

“I want to speak out, because people are not aware of this problem,” Mr Marzec said in an interview with i and Channel 4 News.

“It’s very important for me to speak out, because this illness that I have fallen to – it’s just the beginning.

“I’m sure more and more people will fall ill with it, and unfortunately, it’s an incurable disease.

“Employers set up their companies, but they do not invest in the proper equipment, and what they eventually do is just waste away people’s lives.”

He had moved to the US in 1999 to work as a stonemason there, and recalls good treatment – no work with artificial stone and good safety measures.

Dr Johanna Feary, an occupational lung disease consultant, who is treating kitchen stone workers with silicosis at the Royal Brompton, said there are likely to be many more cases.

In July, i interviewed Malik Al-Khalil, 31, a Syrian refugee, who fled the war-torn country but contracted silicosis after five years cutting quartz in London workshops.

Several concerned artificial stone workers had been in touch with the hospital after i revealed earlier this month that case numbers have doubled.

“This is affecting a range of different patients. It’s not just one small community that’s affected,” Dr Feary said.

“There are likely to be many other patients who will come forward, or people with this disease will be identified in the coming months as public awareness grows.

“We’re really at the tip of the iceberg. I have no idea how many people work with this, and therefore it’s really difficult to put a number on it.

“But the numbers will absolutely increase. That’s what I am certain of.

“I would continue to encourage anyone who has worked with artificial stone and who is concerned about their health to contact us directly using details on our website, or speak to their GP, who can quickly refer them to us at the occupational lung disease service at Royal Brompton for further assessment.”

Ewan Tant, a lawyer for Leigh Day who is representing Mr Marzec, said other clients with silicosis have described similar working conditions, including ineffective masks, no airborne dust monitoring, improper health and safety checks, nor risk assessment.

“These are young men in the prime of their life developing this condition. I first saw Marek in July and since then, it’s been a rapid deterioration,” he said.

“By the time I saw him in July was unable to walk more than a few metres without taking a breath.

“If you look at what happened in California and Australia – where, I think, in a similar sort of timeframe, they had low figures five or six years ago, and are now, in the hundreds of cases – I think we should be concerned that we’re looking at a similar trajectory.”

The law firm wants better awareness of the dangers of engineered stone, improved protection for people working with quartz, as well as tougher regulation of its use, and a funding boost to the Health and Safety Executive to tackle employers with poor practices.
topics: Engineered stone, Silicosis, Subscribers

title: Bedbugs found in Home Office headquarters
body:
Pest control specialists have been treating the site for traces of the parasites, which they believe are being brought in from outside and 'transferred'

The Home Office headquarters in central London is contaminated with bedbugs but civil servants are still being told to use the building, i can reveal.

An investigation by the Government Property Agency (GPA) has found traces of bedbugs in furniture in a building on the Marsham Street complex, which is also home to the Ministry for Housing, Communities and Local Government.

An internal cross-departmental notice, seen by i, said tests from the GPA’s specialist pest control contractors had been carried out “across the campus”.

It stated there was a “further detection of bedbug traces in the Peel building”, suggesting the small insects have previously been found on the site.

The staff notice added that pest control has “sealed and moved affected furniture away as a precautionary measure” and will be carrying out “treatment of the area”.

It added that the parasites are believed to have been “brought in from outside and then transferred around the building”.

The Home Office said the GPA was continuing to monitor the situation but that “all buildings remain safe and open for use”.

Although most people have a mild reaction to the bites, which can be very itchy, others can suffer from a severe allergic reaction and painful swelling.

It is not clear how many traces of bedbugs have been detected or how many items of furniture have been contaminated.

Traces of bedbugs in Home Office furniture were first reported to be found in April but the department told staff that the issue had been resolved.

That came after an outbreak at the government offices in Canary Wharf, where officials from the Ministry of Justice and the UK Security Health Agency work. It led to civil servants being asked to work from home while treatment to eradicate the insects was carried out. This incident led to specially-trained dogs to identify bedbugs ahead of treatment procedures.

Last year, there were fears in London that bedbugs could spread through the capital after an outbreak in Paris where they were reported in schools, trains, hospitals and cinemas. But the UK has long had its own bedbug population and there is no way to know the source of any particular infestation.

Reports of infestations increase in late summer and autumn, which may be partly just because people tend to travel more in summer and then bring home the insects. In winter, bedbugs tend to go into a dormant state if exposed to cooler temperatures, and so cannot travel so well between buildings.

Bedbugs often live in furniture. At home they can live in clothes or sheets and are named after their habit of hiding out in beds, then emerging at night. Their bites leave itchy blotches, which appear red on white skin or purplish on darker skin tones. The bites will usually be on parts of the body that were exposed overnight, like the arms or face.

The insects can be hard to get rid of as they can survive by nestling deep into cracks in furniture.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “There is absolutely no evidence of an infestation on site. The building remains completely safe and open for use.”
topics: Bedbugs, Home Office

title: 'I'm a landlord - capital gains tax rise in Budget would feel like robbery'
body:
'It feels like the Government is picking on people who don’t get much support,' one landlord tells i

Landlords fear they will be forced to sell their properties to cope with the effects of the upcoming Budget if Rachel Reeves goes ahead with raising capital gains tax (CGT).

Earlier this month, it was revealed that the Chancellor is considering raising CGT as high as 39 per cent in the Budget in an effort to increase funds for public services.

The wealth tax is paid by about 350,000 UK taxpayers and is levied on the sale of assets including second homes and shares but at significantly lower rates than wages.

Property owners who make a profit that exceeds their taxable allowance when they sell a property they do not live in are among those who have to pay CGT.

The Prime Minister has suggested people who get their income from assets such as shares and property could be hit with tax rises in this week’s Budget.

Sir Keir Starmer told Sky News that these groups “wouldn’t come within my definition” of working people for whom he has promised not to raise taxes on.

Ahead of the expected changes, some landlords have started selling their rental properties to avoid being hit by a potential increase. An increasing amount of landlords have switched to owning their rental properties as a rental company.

More than 5,000 limited companies were created in Great Britain in September to hold buy-to-let property, a 28 per cent increase year on year, according to research released by Hamptons this month.

Kerry Pace, 61, is an accidental landlord because she has been unable to sell her flat in Sanderstead, south London, after it was discovered to have unsafe cladding and failed its fire safety checks.

Ms Pace told i that she and her husband had planned to buy a new flat in Croydon, south London, that was more suited to their needs, but have been unable to sell their flat for over four years.

“We had no idea at the time that this wouldn’t be resolved quickly – nobody had heard about the cladding issue,” she said. “We thought it would be resolved quickly and, in a few months, we’d be able to sell the flat.”

Ms Pace had already started purchasing her new property in Croydon, so proceeded with the payment by raising money against another property she owns in the area, which she has had for over 20 years.

“That now has a massive mortgage on it and that will be affected by capital gains,” she added.

Ms Pace said she would have sold her Sanderstead flat were it not for its unsafe cladding, and would have also sold the property she has owned for over 20 years were it not for the high CGT she would have to pay.

Keeping both properties meant Ms Pace had to get a mortgage, while her husband cashed in his pension, so they could raise the funds needed to purchase their new Croydon flat.

Commenting on the potential rise of CGT after the Budget, Ms Pace told i: “The whole thing is just robbery. It’s really excessive and I don’t think anybody should pay almost 40 per cent on their capital gains.

“If you buy a property, you’ve invested an awful lot of money into that property and it’s an unnecessarily huge amount of tax. Especially when the situation is out of your control – that makes it doubly unfair.

“It all just feels very personal. People have this perception that landlords have a lot of money lying around. It feels like the Government is picking on people who don’t get much support. They think it’s an easy win.

“Before I came down here, my last job was working in a Jobcentre. I’ve done any job under the sun. I’ve worked all my life. To have the rug pulled out of you this late in life is just gross.”

Jack Malnick, a property expert with 20 years’ experience and founder of SellHouseFast.co.uk, told i the pressure is mounting for landlords, due to anticipated reforms in areas like CGT and inheritance tax relief.

He added that the selling market is seeing particular surges from landlords or second home owners looking to shed assets from their property portfolios.

Mr Malnick said: “Some are already starting to sell off properties, with a 10-year high in buy-to-let sales reported in areas like London. This could lead to a rush of landlords exiting the market by early 2025, causing a surge in property listings as they aim to avoid higher tax burdens.

“There is a 100 per cent increase into SellHouseFast.co.uk and the fast sale market in general. We are seeing record percentages of homes for sale on the open market as well – Rightmove saw 18 per cent of homes in September had previously been rented out vs 8 per cent the year before at the same time.”

Susan Turner, 76, from Cranbrook near Exeter, became a landlord after inheriting properties from her father.

Ms Turner sold one of the properties following divorce and bought a bungalow with a £5,000 mortgage which she paid off within two years.

Ms Turner, who is an independent salesperson for health food and cosmetics company Forever Living, said she is only able to shield herself from the impact of government cuts and tax rises as she is still working.

“There’s very few people that can decide to walk out of the divorce, move into a bed-sit, and look for house of their own,” she said.

Ms Turner has not decided to sell her second home at this time but she is considering making plans to shield herself or her relatives from a rise in CGT.

Her rental property, a one-bed flat, is located near Exeter, within walking distance of the city centre. She charges £750 a month for rent.

“It commands good rent,” Ms Turner said, who has been renting out the property for around 25-30 years. She said changes around CGT would not prompt her to sell immediately but she is looking into her options.

“It probably doesn’t change what I’ll do with the property, but it changes my thoughts about what I need to do,” she said.

“I’m thinking I do need to do something fairly wisely, sooner rather later, and instead of just avoiding the issue, I need to address it.”

The action Ms Turner is considering is transferring the properties into her relatives’ names or switching to joint ownership. An estate does not have to pay any CGT on the property or assets that weren’t sold before the person who owned them died.

But if a property is sold during probate and its value has risen since the person died, there is usually CGT to pay.

Ms Turner is also concerned that landlords are being increasingly targeted by Government polices.

She said: “I find with my rental property, it always seems to be more and more emphasis is put on the people in it – I think, that it’s very difficult for us, as landlords, to have any rights over it.

“I agree that the state of some properties that landlords put tenants into is absolutely atrocious, and I would never want to put an animal in some of them. So I think there needs to be some sort of regulation as to it needs to be a certain standard.”
topics: Budget, Home Ownership, Housing Market, Landlords, Property, Renting

title: Man dies in detention at immigration removal centre near Gatwick
body:
Gatwick Detainees Welfare Group said 'no one should take their last breath' at the centre

A man has died in detention at Brook House immigration removal centre near Gatwick Airport, security company Serco has confirmed.

The company, which manages and operates the detention centre in West Sussex, said a 26-year-old man died on Sunday.

The Home Office said their condolences are with the man’s family and friends.

A spokesperson for the detention centre said: “We can confirm the death of a 26-year-old man at Brook House yesterday.”

It comes almost a year after a 37-year-old Albanian man died after attempting suicide in November 2023 while he was being detained at Brook House.

A public inquiry into the detention centre concluded migrants had been subjected to abuse.

The inquiry found there had been 19 incidents of mistreatment against detainees over a five-month period in 2017.

The government has been criticised over its reaction to the inquiry, with chairwoman Kate Eves – appointed by the then-Conservative government to lead the probe – calling in September for a “reset” on an “inadequate” government response to her recommendations.

The Gatwick Detainees Welfare Group, which supports detainees at Brook House, said “no one should take their last breath” at the centre.

Paying tribute to the man who died, the charity said on X: “On the death of a man in detention yesterday we send heartfelt condolences to his family, friends and everyone who knew and loved him.

“Brook House is prison architecture and no-one should take their last breath there. We mourn that a young man died before he could be free.”

Steve Valdez-Symonds, Amnesty International UK’s refugee and migrant rights director, said: “We despair at reports that yet another person has died in the Brook House detention centre. Our hearts go out to his family, friends and the fellow detainees affected by this tragedy too.

“Brook House has gained notoriety for violence, racism and abuse. What part this may have in this man’s death we do not yet know, but these degradations derive from a wider failure to make a system respect human dignity and rights.

“Tragic incidents such as this emphasise why the Government must bring humanity to the immigration system as much as any other policy area – people’s lives depend on it.”

Medical Justice, which works with vulnerable people in immigration detention, called immigration removal centres (IRCs) “dangerous”.

The charity made reference to Frank Ospina who died last March while he was being detained at Colnbrook immigration removal centre, in West Drayton, Middlesex, pending his removal to Colombia.

An jury at an inquest into his death found that he had died by suicide.

Medical Justice said: “Brook House Inquiry found clinical safeguards in detention to be “dysfunctional” and the systemic failures are ongoing.

“Just a matter of days ago, in response to the inquest into the suicide in immigration detention of Frank Ospina following a catalogue of failings in his care, the Home Office claimed that it has taken a number of actions to improve the safeguards for individuals in detention.

“Medical Justice has little confidence this is the case as we have seen no improvement in safety in detention following many such assurances over the years.”
topics: Gatwick Airport, Immigration, Serco

title: My day in the most pro-Trump town in America
body:
Donald Trump won around 96 per cent of the vote in Miami, Texas. Molly Blackall finds a tight-knit town - and a surge in conspiracy theories

MIAMI, TEXAS – Pronounced Mi-ah-muh by locals, this Miami is a town with more churches than supermarkets, restaurants or hotels.

Located in the Texas Panhandle and surrounded by ranchland, there are only around 700 registered voters and many have lived here all their lives.

Before the last presidential election, it was best known for being home of the national cow-calling contest. But in 2020, it shot to fame when election results revealed it was the most pro-Trump place in America.

More than 96 per cent of voters in Roberts County – of which Miami is the only town – backed Donald Trump – and just 17 ballots were cast for Joe Biden.

It is also one of the more politically engaged communities: turnout stood at more than 80 per cent, significantly higher than the national average of 67.

Over the past four years, Miami has been inundated with reporters from the national and international press – something that has made many locals tire ofthe attention. After pulling up at the junction around which most of the town sits, I approach ten or 15 people for comment who all say a polite no.

I head to the Roberts County museum, an eclectic mixture of town history mostly donated by locals.

Among the wedding dresses and stuffed animals is a commemoration of a darker part of Miami’s past: a charter marking the creation of the town’s branch of the Ku Klux Klan in 1922, when the white supremacist terror group boasted around four million members across the US.

Even today, the lack of diversity in the town is noticeable. There are a handful of Hispanic families but no Black or Asian residents, according to locals.

Upstairs in the museum, a group of elderly women are quilting and agree to let me sit with them. One criticises President Biden for the rising cost of groceries and petrol and expresses concern about the impact of a shift towards net zero in area dependent on the oil industry.

But the overwhelming issue attracting her to Donald Trump is immigration. It is an issue the former president has made central to the US election, as he seeks to paint Kamala Harris as untrustworthy on border security.

Trump has claimed the US has become a “garbage can for the world”, baselessly alleged that Haitian migrants were eating household pets in Ohio, and said that migrants are bringing in “bad genes” and “poisoning the blood of our country”.

It is clear that this anti-migrant rhetoric is striking a chord in communities like Miami.

“A lot of these people that’s come across, they’re not desirable people,” she adds. “It’s not people you want in your community. They’re drug lords and that kind of stuff. Cartels.”

Downstairs at the museum we meet Rick Tennat, a retired county judge who was born in Roberts County in 1953 and now owns a tyre shop in the town. He also says immigration one of the issues driving him towards the Republican Party.

Residents in Miami are still feeling the bite of the high cost of living, he says, and believe “Bidenomics” have not worked. “My taxes are high, groceries cost me almost twice what they did four years ago. I mean, this is ridiculous,” he adds.

Religion is at the core of Miami’s community. Despite its tiny population, there are three churches just minute’s walk apart.

Rachael Davis, 43, moved to the town three-and-a-half years ago with her family. Her husband is the pastor at the first Baptist Church. She stops briefly as she posts a letter nearby and I ask about the election.

“For us it’s not about politics, it’s about winning souls for Christ,” she says.

At the neighbouring church, 66-year-old David Bean is walking up the steps with his wife Amy and their dog, Milly. He welcomes us into the church and out of the baking heat.

A former military man now working in aviation, Mr Bean describes the community as “tight-knit”, “safe” and “salt of the earth”. The town’s residents make it “a priority to vote, because that’s the only thing we’re in control of.”

“I like President Trump because our foes probably think he’s a little bit unpredictable, and so they’re at bay,” he says.

Mr Bean believes Russia – which he calls the Soviet Union – would not have invaded Ukraine if Trump was still in power, nor would the Israel-Hamas war have escalated to such heights.

But he isn’t without his criticisms of the former president: he has been disappointed by Trump’s criminal convictions since the last election.

“What’s kind of disappointing to me is that America takes a lot of this stuff in stride. It came from Bill Clinton and everything. People have proven their misbehaviour, and they turned the other cheek,” he says. “I don’t condone what he did, and by any means, but use the old phrase, ‘lesser of two evils’.”

I ask if the identities of the town’s handful of Democrats are an open secret. “We all know and we disagree with each other, but we don’t talk a lot about politics,” he says. “But I want to hear all sides. Nobody’s picking up or stepping on anybody’s signs. People are acting like adults”.

As the evening draws in, Mr Tennat from the museum invites me to join him and his friends for a dominoes game at his tyre shop on the edge of town. The group gather here almost every day.

John Locke, a 55-year-old businessman, lives in the neighbouring town of Pampa but has land in Miami and comes to the tyre shop most days. He tells us that locals want to lead lives based on conservative values: “We believe in the Bible, morals and values, Jesus Christ, guns and all kinds of stuff.”

But as they swat at flies and drink beer, conversation turns dark.

I ask Joe Lunsford, a 72-year-old rancher who has lived in the town all his life, why the town is the most Republican in the US. “Because we’re good people. We don’t have no coloured people,” he says.

Mr Lunsford goes on to describe Nancy Pelosi, the Democrat Speaker of the House of Representatives and hate figure for the far right, as a “bitch” who “should have been run out” of Congress, and calls for term limits for older politicians like her.

Mr Locke believes that the Capitol attack was an “inside job”.

“It’s out there. You just got to go find it. That’s the problem – the media is run by the Democrats. They’re both in bed together,” he says.

I am not run by the Democrats, I point out.

“Well, our media at least,” he says. “You have to go find the truth, because they don’t give you the truth. It’s hard for me to explain it to y’all, because y’all have no clue. You can go listen to these talk shows and podcasts, read, explore and dig and research about what they’re talking about, and you can find that the government is nothing but a big cabal. It’s a big cover up. Republicans, Democrats, it’s all lies.”

As the conversation progresses, more conspiracy theories creep in.

“They’re not Democrats anymore. They’re trying to get us to where they can rule us and take everything and turn it into socialism, and socialism becomes communism. They’ve been in bed with the Chinese, the Russians and the Middle Easterns the past 70 years,” he says.

It is clear Mr Locke has a fundamental distrust of politicians, claiming they are “funnelling foreign aid back into their coffers” and suggesting Barack Obama was corrupt because his net worth increased sharply after being US president.

It is precisely this that he likes about Trump: “He’s never been in politics before, he’s been a businessman. He made our economy great for four years, he tried to drain the swamp. That’s why they’re so against him, because he figured them out.”

The businessman also repeats regular Trump attack lines about migrants: “Venezuela’s crimes went down; they brought them all over here. They emptied their prisons. They’ve emptied their insane asylums.”

The Venezuelan Observatory of Violence, an independent organisation tracking violence in the country, and FactCheck.org have said they have “no evidence” that this is true.

He then turns to the UK’s own debate around immigration. “Y’all are getting invaded over there right now by all kinds of people, and it’s not too happy,” he says in apparent reference to small boat arrivals. “They’re not too happy are they?”

I try to move the conversation on. “No, that’s a question,” he snaps. “All this stuff is simple. But the problem is, these people try to make it so complicated and throw shade over here and say, pay attention to that.

“We’re heading for another revolution. If the Democrats find a way to lie, steal and cheat again, there’s going to be a confrontation.”

The sun is dimming over the tyre shop and tension is mounting, so I make my exit.

It is clear that in some parts of the town, conspiracy theory has taken hold, and it is difficult to imagine anything which might shake these men’s beliefs.

If Christianity is the most powerful force in Miami, Trumpism might be the second.
topics: Donald Trump, Kamala Harris, Texas, US Election

title: Why do the clocks change? Reason the UK has daylight saving time, explained
body:
On Sunday morning daylight saving time (DST) meant the clocks went back one hour at 2.00am.

With many mourning the loss of long, light summer evenings you might think an extra hour of sleep would soften the blow of the incoming winter.

On Sunday morning daylight saving time (DST) meant the clocks went back one hour at 2.00am.

Each year in the UK, clocks go forward an hour in the March to British Summer Time (BST) and then back an hour in October to Greenwich Mean Time (GMT).

It means sunset will be around one hour earlier and sunrise one hour earlier but the days will continue to get shorter as we head towards the winter solstice.

Although most digital devices now adjust to the time change automatically, any old grandfather clocks will need to be manually turned back to keep you on time.

Now a controversial tradition, DST polarises the nation twice a year with many asking if this outdated system serves the few over the many.

Here is the history of DST, and when the clocks next change, explained.

Contrary to common belief, DST was not implemented for the benefit of farmers, and agriculturalists in fact lobbied against the change when it was first brought in.

In fact, farmers were against DST because caused them to lose valuable morning light and disrupted milking times and impacted both their and their livestock’s health due to enforcing changes in both’s natural rhythms.

US founding father, Benjamin Franklin first proposed the idea of using daylight saving time in a letter he wrote when in Paris in 1784.

But it was not until 1916 when the idea was fully realised. Englishman William Willett, an ancestor of Coldplay’s lead singer Chris Martin, campaigned in 1907 to advance clocks in spring to take advantage of the early daylight and turn them back in the autumn.

Then during the First World War, Germany turned the clocks forward to reduce energy costs and many other European nations followed suit.

Then the Summer Time Act was passed in the UK decreeing that for a certain period during the year legal time should be one hour in advance of GMT.

Daylight saving or summer time is seen as a means to make the most of increased summer daylight hours in the northern hemisphere.

It is argued the change to daylight saving time reduces energy consumption, provides longer evenings for leisure and outdoor exercise and reduces road accidents.

The counterargument is that changing the clocks creates darker mornings, and impacts people’s routines in an age where artificial light is now commonplace.

Although the changeover always happens at a weekend to be least disruptive for schools and businesses, many want the system to stop altogether.

In 2025, the hour changes will take place on Sunday 30 March when clocks will go forward and Sunday 26 October when clocks will go back.

Before 30 October, the clocks last went forward an hour at 1am on the 31 March of this year bringing us into BST, sometimes known as Daylight Saving Time as there is more daylight in the evening and less in the morning.
topics: Clocks, Explainer, Time, Uk

title: Israel bans Palestinian refugee agency UNRWA
body:
The head of the agency said the move 'will only deepen the suffering Palestinians'

Israel’s parliament has passed two laws that could prevent the UN agency for Palestinian refugees from operating in the country, putting the flow of vital aid into Gaza at risk.

The laws ban the UN Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) from operating in Israel, designate it a terror organisation, and cut all ties between the agency and the Israeli government.

Banning UNRWA from operating on Israeli soil would effectively bar it from working in Gaza or the West Bank, as access to both is controlled by Israel.

The agency is the major distributor of aid in Gaza and provides education, health and other basic services to millions of Palestinian refugees across the region.

United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres said banning it could have “devastating consequences” and added he would bring the matter before the UN General Assembly.

The head of UNRWA, Commissioner General Philippe Lazzarini, called the move “unprecedented” and said the bills “will only deepen the suffering Palestinians, especially in Gaza where people have been going through more than a year of sheer hell.”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said UNRWA workers must be held accountable for what he called their “terrorist activities” against the country.

Israel has claimed that hundreds of UNRWA workers are members of Hamas, accusing more than a dozen of participating in the 7 October 2023 attack. The agency, which has 30,000 employees, immediately fired nine staff accused of involvement.

Mr Netanyahu added: “Since avoiding a humanitarian crisis is also essential, sustained humanitarian aid must remain available in Gaza now and in the future.

“In the 90 days before this legislation takes effect – and after – we stand ready to work with our international partners to ensure Israel continues to facilitate humanitarian aid to civilians in Gaza in a way that does not threaten Israel’s security.”

The first vote passed 92-10 and followed a fiery debate between supporters of the law and its opponents, mostly members of Arab parliamentary parties. The second law was approved 87-9.

The bills would come into effect 60 to 90 days after Israel’s foreign ministry notifies the UN, according to the spokesman for politician Dan Illouz, a co-sponsor of one of the bills.

The legislation risks severely affecting the delivery of humanitarian aid into Gaza, where more than 1.9 million Palestinians are displaced from their homes, facing widespread shortages of food, water and medicine.

Hundreds of thousands live in tent camps and schools-turned-shelters, mostly run by UNRWA. Experts say hunger is rampant.

Israel’s military campaign in Gaza since 7 October has killed more than 43,000 Palestinians.

UK Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer said Israel must ensure UNRWA can continue operating in Gaza and deliver its “essential work”.

In a statement on Monday evening, he said: “This legislation risks making UNRWA’s essential work for Palestinians impossible, jeopardising the entire international humanitarian response in Gaza and delivery of essential health and education services in the West Bank.”

US state department spokesman Matthew Miller, speaking to reporters in Washington, said the administration was “deeply concerned” by the legislation.

“There’s nobody that can replace them right now in the middle of the crisis,” he said.

The laws mark the culmination of a long-running campaign against UNRWA, which Israel has accused of harbouring Hamas militants.

UNRWA says it thoroughly investigates any allegations of wrongdoing and holds staff accountable, and that it provides lists of all of its staff to Israel and host countries.

It says Israel has largely ignored its requests to provide evidence for its claims against staffers.

Israel has repeatedly struck UN schools-turned-shelters, claiming Hamas fighters operate inside them.

It also says it has uncovered tunnels running near or under UNRWA facilities.

UNRWA has long been the biggest single employer in Gaza, where the population has been impoverished by years of Israeli and Egyptian blockade.

Hamas has ruled the territory since 2007, and it has civilian political operations alongside its armed wing.

The militant wings of Hamas and other groups are highly secretive, their members virtually unknown outside of intelligence agencies. That complicates efforts by civilian organisations to vet employees.

Fatah Sharif, an UNRWA teacher in southern Lebanon, was killed last month along with his family in an Israeli airstrike.

It then emerged that he was a senior Hamas commander, something he had kept secret.

Mr Lazzarini, UNRWA’s head, said Mr Sharif was suspended without pay in March after the agency learned he belonged to Hamas’s political party, and that an investigation had been launched. He said he did not know Mr Sharif was a militant commander until after his death.
topics: Gaza, Israel, UN

title: Lebanon's 'badass' airline dodges bombs to provide last regular Beirut flights
body:
As bombs fall only streets away from Beirut's airport, Middle East Airlines has become a symbol of national pride and resilience

As Israel has escalated air strikes against Lebanon, bombs have fallen steadily closer to Beirut’s Rafic Hariri airport, forcing airlines to pull out one by one.

However, there is one notable exception: Middle East Airlines (MEA). Lebanon’s national carrier is the last to operate something like a regular schedule in and out of the country, providing a lifeline for the beleaguered population.

Images of its planes taking off and landing through the smoke of bomb blasts in the capital have gone viral, prompting fears for passenger safety, praise for the pilots’ courage, and pride in a symbol of the country struggling through the chaos.

“Badass Middle East Airlines continue landing despite heavy Israeli bombardment around the airport,” Maha Yahya, director of the Carnegie Middle East Centre, wrote on social media last week.

“MEA…is often rightly criticised for everything from corruption to subpar service but at the moment, as the only airline flying in and out of Beirut, it also encapsulates the spirit of a people,” observed Lebanese journalist Rania Abouzeid.

Preston Clarke, an American citizen who flew out of Beirut on an MEA flight during recent weeks of bombardment, told i: “It’s a model of the Lebanese spirit of resilience, what they are doing. I think they’re courageous. They stayed by their post as it were. They were doing their job through it all.”

With air strikes on areas visibly close to the airport, the sight of planes taking off and landing is unnerving. But a senior executive at the airline told i that even during the war, popular fears of threats to MEA’s planes or the airport were overblown.

“People like to exaggerate,” said Captain Mohammed Aziz, adviser to MEA chairman Mohamad el-Hout. “We have assurances from major players that they will not approach the airport, they will not approach an aircraft in flight and this is what makes us really take off and land in such a situation.”

And yet the airline is undoubtedly operating in a high-risk environment. Mr Clarke said it was palpable how close the danger was while he was waiting for his flight.

“We got to the gate and that’s when we could really start hearing explosions… The ground was shaking. Explosions were happening right there by the airport.

“Every 30 seconds, minute, two minutes, you’d hear an explosion or a couple together. But it was muffled, it was like in the distance. We knew it was only a few kilometres away at most.”

Eric Schouten, founder and CEO of the security intelligence organisation Dyami, said that while he wouldn’t advise Western airlines to fly to Lebanon right now, MEA was likely taking mitigating actions to continue flying.

“They need to have a different risk appetite than a Western airline. Which is not per se, bad,” he said.

“It’s not in the interest of Israel to shoot down an airliner. And who is in control of the airspace basically, that’s Israel… If they are in touch, [MEA] can put that in their risk assessments.”

Mr Aziz said that MEA did not hear from Israel directly, but rather from interlocutors like the US, UK and France. Likewise with Hezbollah, he said the Lebanese government was a vital source of information. Regular interactions like these allow the airline to continue operating flights.

“Any time they have any news, any change, they will immediately advise us and we do a daily risk assessment. We evaluate what happened, where the strikes were, how far they were, what the impact of the operation was,” he said.

But Mr Aziz is keen to stress that the airline does not take off and land while air strikes are taking place.

“Aircraft cannot fly through smoke… The attacks in Lebanon are to the east of the airport and most of the wind in Lebanon is westerly wind, so rarely do we have smoke over the airport.

“Either the strike would have taken place before we land or they will strike after we land.”

The airline also needs staff who are able to stomach a higher risk of travelling to and from the airport. While some of MEA’s employees have fled to the mountains or abroad, Mr Aziz said most of the workforce remained in place.

“It’s a very small percentage, about 3 or 4 per cent, of the ground crew. The flight crew is flying daily… If there is fear, they do not fly. The staff trust the self assessment that we do. They feel pride in what they are doing. I cannot call them heroes – we don’t want heroes. We want professional people taking calculated risk.”

Some Lebanese have expressed anger at the prices that MEA has charged in recent weeks for its flights out the country. Reports of flight costs reaching thousands of dollars have been a regular complaint for foreign nationals to their embassies, who have repeatedly asked citizens to leave via commercial options. But Mr Aziz said the airline was making significant losses just to keep operating.

“There is no way you can make money when you have 20 per cent of your fleet sitting outside.”

The airline has been situating some of its planes outside the country, incurring parking fees in cities like Cairo in Egypt, Istanbul in Turkey, Larnaca in Cyprus and Amman in Jordan, in order to maintain the vital insurance it needs to keep operating. While flights out of Lebanon are departing full, flights into the country are arriving mostly empty, sustaining additional losses.

“But we feel we have a duty as Middle East Airlines to maintain this link between Lebanon and the outside world,” Mr Aziz said.

And for those who have relied on the airline in recent weeks and months to get out, it has been a source of comfort.

“They were heroes. We thanked them and the attendants profusely,” said Jonathan Hastings, who flew out with his family in October. Mr Clarke and his family feel similarly.

“They apologised for the simpler refreshments on board than the usual fare. They said it was because of the security circumstances. That really moved me. I just thought, wow, these guys are working through impossible circumstances,” Mr Clarke said.

“They carried on their duty through really difficult, harrowing circumstances. So, it’s admirable and we’re grateful to them.”
topics: Air Travel, Airlines, Beirut, Hezbollah, Israel, Lebanon

title: Donald Trump might have just derailed his own campaign
body:
What a night in New York City. A night that will go down in American political history: as a parade that spoke of confidence in the days before a crushing victory, or a hubristic misstep which derailed that victory.

The Wall Street Journal called Donald Trump’s Madison Square Garden jamboree on Sunday night, “part rock show, part revival; at once dark and grievance-laden yet often comedic and epically long”.

It was a fair summary of an event that was pure Trump. There was indeed plenty of darkness. A comedian who warmed up the crowd described Puerto Rico as an “island of garbage”. Grant Cardone, a businessman, said Vice-President Kamala Harris and “her pimp handlers will destroy our country”, a characterisation archly described in The Washington Post as “a metaphor that casts the Democratic presidential nominee as a prostitute”.

For good measure David Rem, a childhood friend of Trump, called Harris “the devil” and “the Antichrist”.

And then the Donald took to the stage calling the election next week “liberation day” from what he described as an occupation by invading migrants.

It was all very confident. In style – though obviously not substance – it reminded some British viewers of a highly caffeinated version of Labour’s Sheffield rally in 1992.

That rally – of which Trump and most Americans will be blissfully unaware – was in the run up to the 1992 election in the English city of Sheffield, in which Neil Kinnock and his deputy Roy Hattersley seemed to get ahead of their skies when it came to winning the general election which was a week away. It has been credited (probably unfairly) with destroying a polling lead and ending Kinnock’s chances of getting into No 10. Whatever the truth of the impact on the poll it certainly did Kinnock no favours.

Has Trump similarly bombed? There is certainly a case to be made that this was a reckless piece of political theatre. The Puerto Rico comments in particular seem as unwise as they were unpleasant: the key swing state of Pennsylvania has one of the biggest Puerto Rican communities of any state in the union. There are more than 615,000 eligible Latino voters in the state, according to the independent Pew Research Centre and roughly half of them are Puerto Rican. The poll in Pennsylvania could be settled by just tens of thousands of votes on either side and the candidate who wins the 19 electoral college votes there is highly likely to win the election.

So it was not long before the Trump team were doing something they very seldom do: apologising.

“This joke does not reflect the views of president Trump,” Danielle Alvarez, a senior adviser to the campaign, said in a statement.

Republican Senator Rick Scott of Florida, which is home to the largest population of Puerto Ricans in the United States mainland, went further: “This joke bombed for a reason. It’s not funny and it’s not true,” the senator and former Florida governor posted on X. Scott is up for re-election and did not approve of his potential supporters being treated in this way.

The problem for the Democrats is that the perceived recklessness and darkness of the rally may have been blocked out of many minds by the pro-Trump advertising campaign that has been widely regarded as disciplined and focused and totally un-Trump like. These advertisements do not make big news stories, but they are seen by huge numbers of Americans watching football games on TV or looking at clips on social media.

One in particular stays in the mind. It focuses on the faces – multiracial and not angry looking – of men. The commentary says, “Let’s get one thing crystal clear: the vast majority of American men have no issue with electing a female president”.

But it goes on to talk of Harris’s time as attorney general of California and the efforts she made to prosecute the parents of people who allowed their children to skip school. They have clips of her talking proudly of her “tough on crime” policy. Some with her giggling. And clips of the parents who suffered as a result including a black woman who says she was arrested because her handicapped daughter missed some days of school. It is gut-wrenching – whatever the rights and wrongs of a long-forgotten policy, it portrays Harris as unpleasant and hypocritical. It hits home.

And here is the thing: Donald Trump probably hasn’t even seen it. The truancy ad has been paid for by people outside his campaign, a group called Make America Healthy Again. These are the so called “super PACs” – political action committees that have unlimited spending potential and are usually funded by backers who want to pack a punch but stay out of the limelight.

Along with the advertisements the candidate himself has had the wisdom to appear in non-shouty environments, in particular podcasts where he talk at length but without seeming too aggressive. The best of these appearance was on the hugely popular Joe Rogan show – in which he talked among other things about UFOs, his excellent health and what he said behind the scenes to various world leaders. It was cosy Trump.

Who will win this battle for hearts and minds: Trump or Trump. The man himself at his set piece public appearances, ill-disciplined and self-aggrandising, versus his own wealthy backers, who keep in the shadows and use rapiers not bludgeons to make the case for the former president and his team who set up the meetings where he can look approachable and human.

Do people look at the Madison Square Garden event and recoil, or do they look at the advertising and the podcasts and feel that Trump is a better bet, against a woman who is untrustworthy? I guess we shall find out next week.

Justin Webb presents the Americast podcast on BBC Sounds
topics: Donald Trump, Subscribers, US Election, US Politics, USA

title: Jeremy Clarkson proves that, ultimately, we all choose a long life over hedonism
body:
Jeremy Clarkson could never be accused of “optimism bias”, today’s polite term for lying to your doctor about how much you drink or smoke. When Clarkson’s doctor asked him about his alcohol intake, he freely admitted he would drink “three or four pints” a day. Pause. “Of wine,” he’d add, presumably with a dramatic flourish. I have been in his company enough times to confirm that this was a realistic estimate.

During Covid, he joked he feared being reported to the authorities for having hosted a number of illegal parties at his house. No, he’d have to say. The vast number of empty bottles carted away by the recycling lorry had merely been for personal use.

Such a regime would inevitably take its toll, and so it was that, as Clarkson himself said, “the grim reaper poked his nose round the door” recently, and what appeared to we onlookers as a modern miracle – how could a man drink so much, eat so unhealthily and work so hard have so much energy and life force? – turned out to be something of a mirage.

After a series of wobbles that would put any of us on red alert – mobility issues, chest pains, pins and needles in his arms – Clarkson went for tests, and was discovered to have seriously compromised arteries, his mortality most definitely in question. And so he finds himself on a health regime that precludes alcohol, meat, chocolate, and indeed anything for which a sybarite like him might live.

He now complains that kale is “like eating the contents of a AAA battery” and that Greek yoghurt is like “the cheese found in a homeless person’s ­genitals”, but here’s the interesting bit. He doesn’t regret an iota of the erstwhile excess that has got him to this point, using a Top Gear metaphor to explain his philosophy on life: you put your foot to the boards “until you run out of fuel”. Then you buy a “Tesla Lib Dem lifestyle. When you no longer have a choice”.

I’m not sure how socially acceptable Clarkson’s manifesto for living is. Isn’t it an individual’s responsibility not to burden the NHS with their own predilection for reckless consumption? This idea may be dismissed as woke nonsense, and, in an increasingly atomised society, it’s a proposition that probably won’t get much purchase. Forget all that “Protect the NHS” stuff we were told. And the nanny state can bugger off. I’ve got a bottle of rosé to finish.

One of my old friends used to say, while raising a large Johnnie Walker: “A short life, but a happy one.” His life was, sadly, cut short, but he always gave the impression of being happy throughout it.

Times have changed, however, and establishing the balance between longevity and fulfilment is one which now occupies the thoughts of most people over, say, 60 years old.
