As far as it relates to the 64-year-old Clarkson, this dichotomy can be expressed thus: what’s the point of living longer if it means you can’t do any of the things that give you pleasure? But, faced with this invidious choice, even Clarkson himself said: “I decided that, actually, I quite fancied living a little bit longer.” Most of us would come to the same conclusion.

And that’s partly why Ozempic is the most sought-after drug in the world. It’s effectively a mind-altering substance which encourages you to cut out the things that cause you to put on weight (i.e. anything you might enjoy) without the feeling that you’re missing out. It doesn’t work for everyone, but as shortcuts go, it’s pretty effective. Clarkson’s doctor also advised him to take up golf. “I’d rather take up public masturbation,” was how he responded to me.

Jeremy Clarkson, however, is possibly beyond Ozempic, or indeed golf, but one of the most influential people in public life (look at what he’s done to illuminate the struggles of farmers) can now set an example to those of us for whom hedonism has always been an attractive option.

Will he become a poster boy for virtuous living? Doubtful, I’d say. But while his heart may not be in it, at least it’s still there, ticking away.
topics: Diet, Drinking, Health, Healthy Eating, Jeremy Clarkson, Ozempic

title: The tax rise Labour MPs are growing increasingly worried about
body:
For a Prime Minister pitch-rolling a Budget that will define the UK political landscape for the next decade, Sir Keir Starmer’s speech in Birmingham was more impressionist Claude Monet than paint by numbers.

Only occasionally did a brief glimpse of what a future Britain may look like emerge from the picture the Prime Minister sketched today. A blanket promise to “prevent devastating austerity” in public spending was the surest signal yet of the tax hikes and spending cuts worth £40 billion voters are aware are coming on Wednesday.

Amid the impressionism came occasional painterly daubs of light as Starmer made a couple of announcements. Unusually for a Prime Minister, there were some specific if scattergun announcements which should have been saved for Parliament, a decision that irked House of Commons Speaker Lindsay Hoyle. Starmer promised £240m to encourage people back into work, a boon to voters concerned about what the Tories used to call “shirkers” and the economic implications of the growing number of people out of work due to ill health – soaring by 300,000 a year.

In Birmingham the premier didn’t let up on his ongoing rhetoric about “working people” despite the difficulties he and other ministers have got into when explaining what that means. The reason a definition matters is that it gives a clear sense of Labour’s priorities both for this Budget and the future. Presumably an offshore tax accountant feels they do an honest day’s work just as much as a window-cleaner does. They might feel differently after Wednesday.

Minister after minister has spent the last fortnight offering their own definitions. Anyone expecting Starmer to emulate LS Lowry and paint an explicit but sentimental portrait of stick men on their way t’mill was to be disappointed. The Prime Minister said working people of Britain “know exactly who they are”.

Working people “do the right thing”, may be able to “save a little bit of money”, but end up “stuck on NHS waiting lists” and “can’t afford decent housing”, he said. More broadly they’re people who suffer when governments fail. As portraits go, this wasn’t the most definitive.

Starmer said his concern was making sure “there is no more tax” in the payslip for working people, but sidestepped a question about whether a fuel duty rise would count as a tax on those very people who use their cars to get to and from work.

Labour MPs are increasingly worried about a rise to fuel duty. They fear the policy will filter through to their constituents in an easy to understand way. One MP told i that a rise to employer national insurance contributions wouldn’t immediately show up in payslips and therefore was to be favoured – although it could prompt a hiring slowdown in smaller firms. The MP said the party had been stung by the damage the simple decision to means test winter fuel payments has caused.

Starmer said he hopes that “pretty well all” of the biggest tax rises under his leadership will come in this year’s Budget but couldn’t “give you a cast-iron guarantee that in no future Budget will there be an adjustment of tax”, he said, pointing to the experience of the pandemic and Ukraine war as proof that sometimes events blow plans off course. No hostage to fortune here.

Labour, he argued, had no choice but to deliver unpopular tax rises and spending cuts, placing the blame squarely on his Conservative predecessors for the ailing public finances and challenging them to explain what they would do differently.

The decision to give a speech was itself an acknowledgement his Government has been slow in setting out a narrative for the “why” of the Budget, as well as the “what” is in it. Starmer aimed to make that clearer – some taxes will rise, but for the purpose of spending more on public services. It came down to a plea: stick with me, and there will be a fixed NHS and economic growth at the end of it all. Squint and you can see a picture emerging.

“Look – nobody wants higher taxes, just like nobody wants public spending cuts,” Starmer said. “But we have to be realistic about where we are as a country. This is not 1997, when the economy was decent but public services were on their knees. And it’s not 2010, where public services were strong, but the public finances were weak. We have to deal with both sides of that coin.”

Nonetheless, Starmer’s speech was the warm-up to Chancellor Rachel Reeves on Wednesday. However much he tried to paint a picture of a brighter future, the markets are still waiting for the full-scale of the painting to emerge. It’s her macroeconomic photorealism the financial markets are waiting for. Memories of former prime minister Liz Truss’s doomed efforts to stimulate the economy still make Treasury officials shudder. Starmer namechecked her twice in his speech.

UK government borrowing costs rose in response to her signals that she intends to borrow more. The international money traders want reassurances over the extent of her plans. Last week, Reeves confirmed the UK could borrow as much as £70bn more over the next five years, banking on that borrowing to invest in infrastructure won’t spook the bond markets.

“The tough stuff is coming in this Budget,” Starmer promised on Monday. So far, so impressionistic. Wednesday will determine if the picture both he and Reeves have painted is clear enough.
topics: Budget, Fuel Duty, Keir Starmer, Labour Party, Rachel Reeves, UK Politics

title: The demolition of Britain’s greatest man cave is a loss for the brotherhood
body:
Like many men, I felt a sharp pang of pain upon reading the news of Graham Wildin, who has been forced to demolish what had been dubbed as ‘“Britain’s best man cave”. True, it was built illegally. True, Wildin ignored the advice of several council officers to construct it, and then spent close to a full decade – some of it spent in prison – haplessly trying to fend off its destruction. True, his neighbours all seem unanimously delighted about its removal, in part because it was a genuine eyesore.

And yet something about this story feels deeply upsetting. The demolition of a man cave – any man cave – feels like a loss to the collective brotherhood.

This is partly because Wildin’s man cave pushed the boundaries of the term to breaking point. It had a cinema in it. It had a bowling alley in it. There was literally a casino inside the thing. It was 10,000 square feet in size and dwarfed his actual house, which makes it less a cave and more an out-and-out warehouse. Had Wildin wanted, he probably could have stashed a few full aeroplanes in there. You’re right to be jealous.

Because deep down, his complex speaks to something that everyone wishes that they had. A place of their own, to do whatever they like. Especially during Covid, where families suddenly found themselves competing with multiple people for any flat surface from which to work, the thought of having a dedicated space that belonged to nobody but you was the most appealing thing on Earth.

In that regard I’m quite lucky, because I have that. Like Graham Wildin, I have elbowed out some space for myself in my back garden. Unlike Wildin, my shed is completely legal and also only big enough to squeeze a desk and an exercise bike into.

It’s there because I work from home, and it was considerably cheaper than buying a house with enough rooms for everyone. My shed is swelteringly hot in the summer and freezing cold in the winter. The inclusion of the bike means that it very often honks like old socks. And yet I love it dearly.

My shed isn’t like the rest of my house, which is ultimately a compromise between four wildly different people, one of whom has ADHD and another is a seven-year-old boy whose greatest desire is to cover the entire floor with several successive layers of Godzilla toys. No, my shed is mine to do whatever I like with. It’s a refuge, both starkly utilitarian and slightly messy, and as such has become a perfect reflection of my personality.

But then this is true of all similar spaces. Take Graham Wildin. You could look at his man cave, essentially a crèche that had been decorated to look exactly like a Conservative Club from 1983, and get a perfect read on how the man views the world.

These spaces are perfect because they’re self-contained. Had either of us decided to kit out the entirety of our own homes like this – had we decided to make our entire living area a perfect mirror of our inner lives – then any visitor would probably instantly think “Uh-oh, serial killer.” But contained to one room, one shed, one terrifyingly overcompensatory illegally built leisure complex, it’s fine. It’s breathing space. It’s necessary, even.

Because it is important to point out that man caves are not only for men. Everyone wants a space of their own, a place where they can briefly be allowed to hide from expectation and do as they please. A friend of mine has just spent ages fitting out a shed with sofas and a projector, so that she can watch films with her boyfriend in the evening. And when my younger brother moved out of home, my mum almost instantly decided to transform his old bedroom into a place where she could hang up pictures of fairies and furnish a load of doll’s houses. We would all be so much happier if we had somewhere like this to go.

Hopefully Graham Wildin won’t be disheartened by this news. Maybe he can rebuild his man cave smaller and more legally, perhaps without the full-size bowling alley or horrible carpets. Because the important thing isn’t the size of the place. The important thing is that he has room where he can be himself. May we all have such a thing.
topics: Homes, Men

title: There is a weird love-in going on between Donald Trump and WWE
body:
Donald Trump has all the makings of a great professional wrestler. He loves his entrance music (sometimes even forgoing entire rallies so he can stand there and listen to his playlist); he cuts a great promo on his opponents; and a lot of his fans don’t seem able to tell the difference between fiction and reality.

His connections to the wrestling industry run deep. WrestleMania IV and V were held at Trump Plaza; Trump himself appeared as an on-screen character in WrestleMania XXIII’s “Battle of the Billionaires” against company owner Vince McMahon; and he was even inducted into the prestigious WWE Hall of Fame.

Take that, Kamala – I bet you don’t even know what makes a German suplex different from a normal suplex.

So it’s no great surprise that his 2024 campaign has found itself repeatedly intersecting with the world of wrestling. What is a little surprising, though, is just how deep those connections have become, to the point that WWE – and professional wrestling in general – seems to have inadvertently become a core player in Trump’s re-election strategy.

At Trump’s rally in Madison Square Garden on Sunday, Hulk Hogan – a man who made the Garden his wrestling home in the 1980s – made a special appearance to endorse his fellow WWE Hall of Famer for president. The Hulkster used the event to address the assembled “Trump-a-maniacs”, telling them: “I don’t see no stinking Nazis in here. I don’t see no stinking domestic terrorists in here. The only thing that I see in here are a bunch of hard-working men and women that are real Americans, brother.”

The star of Mr Nanny and Santa with Muscles called Kamala Harris a “bad actress”, and advocated for “peace through strength” in the Middle East. He also trotted out one of his many iconic catchphrases – “Whatcha gonna do?” – and claimed that after 40 years of asking the question, he’s finally found his answer: vote for Trump, brother.

It isn’t the first time the former WWE Champion has stumped for Trump – he also made a surprise appearance at this year’s Republican National Convention, which ended with Hogan dramatically ripping off his shirt to reveal a Maga shirt underneath. He tried a similar move at this Sunday’s rally, but struggled to complete the tear, leading to one final wrestling match for the red-faced icon against his greatest opponent yet: cheap Chinese manufacturing.

Hogan’s “special guest” status at these events might strike you as strange, and not just because it’s a man in a feather boa screaming about body slamming people. He’s an icon in wrestling circles, sure, but he doesn’t exactly hold a lot of cultural capital anymore. For him to get not one, but two special guest spots during what may be the most consequential campaign cycle of our lifetimes, feels a bit much – even if he is the second-longest reigning WWE Champion in history.

Perhaps it speaks to the paucity of celebrity endorsements on the right – I’m sure if Hogan hadn’t been available, Kevin Sorbo could have stood in. Or maybe it has something to do with Hogan’s connections to right-wing billionaire Peter Thiel, who bankrolled the Hulkster’s lawsuit against Gawker in the mid-2010s, and is currently acting as patron to Trump’s running mate and alleged couch enthusiast, JD Vance. Who’s to say?

Whatever the reason, Hogan isn’t the only retired wrestling legend to endorse The Donald. Trump also recently appeared on The Undertaker’s podcast, Six Feet Under, where the two men discussed such crucial topics as immigration, transgender athletes in women’s sports, and whether ’Taker could beat Haystacks Calhoun in a fight.

It’s a bizarre little interview that at times feels like a lazy SNL parody – at one point Trump even muses as to why he’s doing this “stupid show” after turning down an interview with 60 Minutes, and to be honest, I’d love to know the answer myself.

The episode isn’t even doing that well – it only has about 650k views on YouTube. That’s fewer than Undertaker’s interview with the wrestler Maven. Remember Maven? Me neither!

Professional wrestling is going through a bit of a resurgence – WWE is selling out stadiums worldwide, and for the first time in ages your co-workers might actually be able to name a wrestler who didn’t retire two decades ago.

But it’s still pretty niche. Trump is out here hitching his wagon to guys who have taken more chair shots to the head than you’ve had hot dinners, and for what? Is there some polling data out there that says the jabroni bloc is key to swinging Pennsylvania?

Wrestling has always been a pretty right-wing industry. Vince McMahon’s wife Linda served on Trump’s cabinet, and current CCO Paul Levesque, aka Triple H, wasn’t shy about having his picture taken with Trump, despite being less outspoken about politics in general.

George Murdoch, formerly WWE’s Brodus Clay (aka the “Funkasaurus”) is a regular contributor on Fox News. Even The Undertaker’s former tag team partner Glenn Jacobs, aka Kane, is a staunch Trump advocate, who has served as the Republican mayor of Knox County, Tennessee since 2018 (he is also, despite playing a silent masked character for much of his career, a vocal anti-masker).

It’s not just the old-timers, either – Trump supporters can be found right across wrestling’s generational divide. WWE’s developmental division, NXT, is rumoured to be full to the brim with pro-Trump sentiment despite being largely composed of Gen Z athletes.

Nikkita Lyons, 25, is informally known as “Maga Thee Stallion” by fans, after posting an Instagram video set to a song justifying the 6 January insurrection. Logan Paul, who has been signed with WWE since 2022, is extremely vocal about his support. He even hosted Trump on his (marginally more successful) podcast Impaulsive this past June while still US Champion, allowing Trump to hold his title belt. Even the current WWE Champion, Cody Rhodes, was linked to a Trump-supporting Twitter account in 2016 (though he has since denied being “Maga” when asked directly).

In many ways, wrestling really is the last bastion of conservativism in mainstream entertainment – which is ironic, since according to polls, WWE has one of the most comparatively liberal fanbases in all of sport. That propensity rarely makes its way to the screen, and wrestlers’ personal affiliations tend only to come out once they’re safely retired, but when you compare it with things like Hollywood and the television industry, it’s the closest thing the right has to an ideological safe haven.

It also presents a rare opportunity for the GOP to reach out to those younger voters who might naturally be inclined to vote Democrat – although whether or not any first-time 20-something voters are going to switch to the red team because Ted Dibiase tells them to is another matter. Personally, I think they’re more likely to be turned off supporting their favourite wrestler than they would be inclined to follow them, but a celebrity endorsement is a celebrity endorsement. Just ask Kevin Sorbo.

That’s why Trump is so drawn to it, I think. Donald is a showman at heart, but he’s been roundly rejected by pretty much every mainstream cultural force for his abhorrent views. He’ll never get an endorsement from Taylor Swift or Beyoncé, and he’s not going to be invited to the Tonys, so if he wants the pageantry and spectacle that he craves, all that’s left for him are big men with big muscles and bigger personalities.

Of course he’s embraced wrestling – what else is he going to do, brother?
topics: Donald Trump, Kamala Harris, Professional Wrestling, WWE

title: Pope faces last chance with England as Cox and Bairstow wait in the wings
body:
Under fire No 3 is on borrowed time after a wretched run of form

ISLAMABAD — The contortions England have got themselves into over Ollie Pope’s position at No 3 following a horrendous series in Pakistan was best illustrated by the fact they have delayed naming the squad for their upcoming tour of New Zealand.

Initially, this was meant to drop the day the series here finished. However, the collapse that led to the surrender in the deciding Test inside two-and-a-half days meant the squad for the series against the Black Caps was put on the back burner.

It doesn’t take much imagination to deduce that the manner of that defeat in Rawalpindi probably prompted Rob Key, England’s director of cricket, to tell coach Brendon McCullum and captain Stokes that they needed a conversation once they were both home before making anything public.

Given McCullum 18 hours in Qatar before flying another 18 hours or so back to Auckland on his journey home, the delay is understandable.

But you don’t need to be Sherlock Holmes to work out the focus of those conversations – Pope, a man whose up-and-down 2024 reached a new low in Pakistan as he averaged 11 in the series.

Both Stokes and McCullum backed Pope to the hilt after the final Test. “There is no doubt in my mind and no doubt in Brendon’s mind that we have the got the best top-six players in England,” Stokes said. “You can’t shut the door on everything.”

McCullum added: “I’ve said it heaps, No 3 is a tough place to bat. Popey is disappointed with his output of runs here, no doubt. He came into the series hitting the ball as well as anyone in the nets. His confidence was strong.

“It wasn’t to be for Popey in this series, but it was only a couple of Tests ago he got a brilliant 150 for us. He’ll benefit from a couple of weeks out and he’ll get another opportunity when we head to New Zealand in conditions where he’ll hopefully be able to flourish.”

Pope’s 154 actually came four Tests ago against Sri Lanka at The Oval to ease the pressure that was on him at the time. It was ever thus. He is a player’s whose infrequent big scores always quieten the frenzied speculation over his position. Until the next time.

McCullum is right when he says No 3 is a difficult place to bat. It’s why Pope probably shouldn’t be there.

England’s next two series after New Zealand are India at home and Australia away. Can Pope really be the man to take down the two best attacks in the world? His average of 22 against them suggests not.

It was apparent that standing in as captain when Stokes was injured for the Sri Lanka series at the end of the summer and the first Test in Pakistan did affect his form.

But there is now huge pressure on Pope to produce big runs in New Zealand if, as seems likely, he makes the squad.

Despite the backing from McCullum and Stokes, it’s not hard to imagine that Key – the third selector for England – has warned them it’s New Zealand or bust for the Surrey man.

There is no doubt the observations on Pope from former England captains Michael Vaughan and Nasser Hussain in recent days have caught the attention of Key.

As i also suggested last week, both Hussain and Vaughan floated the idea in their respective newspaper columns of Stokes batting at No 3 if Pope was dropped.

Vaughan, though, went one step further and zeroed in on Pope’s technical and temperamental flaws to argue why he should be dropped. Writing in the Telegraph, the 2005 Ashes-winning skipper said: “Test cricket changes over time, and this England have changed it plenty. But one thing I really do not think has changed is that the No 3 must be a pillar of calm and control. Pope does not seem to be able to soak up difficult periods.

“I have said before I think Pope has a fragile mentality. He is not alone in that. But when your mentality is fragile, you need your technique to fall back on. It looks after you on your bad days, which there are a lot more of than good ones in Test cricket.

“If Pope and England are honest with themselves, they have to recognise even his best innings have lacked control. One thing I am certain of is that Australia and India would love to see him walking out at No 3 next year.”

New Zealand seems like a tipping point for Pope. Afterwards there is a five-month break before England play Test cricket again. The series will also present an opportunity to Jordan Cox, who is expected to come into the team as wicketkeeper for at least the final two Tests when Jamie Smith heads home on paternity leave.

If Cox does well and Pope’s poor run continues, it could be the end of the line for the 26-year-old. Stokes or even Joe Root might be asked to move up to three in that scenario to fit Cox into the middle come next summer.

Even if Cox bombs, Pope needs runs. Otherwise maybe there could even be a way back for Jonny Bairstow or Dan Lawrence ahead of those series against India and Australia?

Pope should at least benefit from the typically flat pitches New Zealand produce for home Tests. Yet given his recent form, nothing can be taken for granted.
topics: England Cricket, Jonny Bairstow, Ollie Pope

title: Ten Hag sacking leaves Man Utd in a mess - and one man is to blame above all
body:
“I told you so” echoes around the football firmament. Opposing fans have been cantillating Erik ten Hag with the death song, “you are getting sacked in the morning” since the spring, when the record number of defeats in a Premier League season were racking up.

The surprise, of course, is not that he has gone but that it has taken Manchester United so long to accept his failings, which points a neon arrow at the crack unit assembled to rebuild the fallen giant. Monday was self-evidently a painful moment for Ten Hag, but perhaps more so for the guru squad brought in to reinvent the wheel.

At the top of the Old Trafford pyramid sits Ineos owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe. Ultimately responsibility rests with him but since he is the most powerful figure at the club, the one with all the gold, no-one is going to give him his cards. Next in line sits guru-in-chief Sir Dave Brailsford, the god of small things who occupies the throne at the top of the Ineos sporting pyramid dispensing Delphic wisdom like Zeus, or should that be Dr Seuss?

Brailsford was among the group leading the search for a new manager before deciding Ten Hag had indeed passed the leadership review in the summer. Had they begun the process earlier Ineos might have saved a few bob flying about the parish interviewing candidates like Thomas Tuchel, Roberto De Zerbi, Thomas Frank, Kieran McKenna etc. Perhaps it was the weekender at Ten Hag’s pad in Ibiza that swung the day. I mean, who doesn’t like a beach party?

The greater Brailsford’s football imprint grows the more he triggers comparisons with Sir Clive Woodward, a guru from a distant epoch and like Brailsford, a different sport, whose expertise was gobbled up by Southampton. England’s World Cup winning rugby coach was given the role of technical director in the summer of 2005. The appointment was always viewed with suspicion by manager Harry Redknapp, who lasted six months before escaping down the Solent to Portsmouth.

Six months after that, Southampton’s owner Rupert Lowe sold up, removing the glue that kept Woodward in power. Barely 12 months after beginning the Southampton revolution, the “mad professor” as Woodward became known by staff, was gone, taking up a post at the British Olympic Association.

Brailsford’s protector loves him, so he comfortably avoids the fate of Ten Hag. United’s new CEO Omar Berrada and the club’s new sporting director, Dan Ashworth, took up their roles in the post-season and would like to shrug “nowt to do with me guv”. Except they can’t, because the evidence was there before them whether they were in situ or not.

Even in the deepest corners of the respective gardens in which both passed their leave from Manchester City and Newcastle United, there was no escape from the dire telemetry of Ten Hag’s second season. The decision they came to on Monday morning in Carrington was available to them in May, but the club fell for the illusion that a one-off win against City in the FA Cup final was significant. Well Ten Hag would claim that, wouldn’t he?

Instead they assembled in a cluster and rolled out a party line of unity and support. He’s our man, they said, ignoring the prior search for a better version. Thus did Monday’s ever-so cordial sacking delivered by Berrada and Ashworth condemn both twice over. If he was the “right” choice in the summer, he remains so now because neither the conditions nor the circumstances have changed. Of course he wasn’t, as the search for a successor proved.

It is almost possible to feel sorry for Ten Hag, a decent man who trusted what his bosses were telling him, that they were on the same page, in this together, moving forward, committed to him. The poor sap was still peddling his delusions after the defeat at West Ham, claiming sincerely that United turned last season around with that one win in May, and would do so again.

Ye gods. Interestingly the pattern of that game was not unlike Sunday’s across the capital. The difference being United netted in the first half at Wembley when the force was with them, which provided the insurance during the second half when it was not.

We don’t need to revisit the anatomy of Ten Hag’s failings. ChatGPT would suffice for that, rounding up the lethal stats in a thrice, the colossal waste of £650m in player recruitment, the unprecedented defeats, added time goals conceded, paucity of goals scored, etc. No, the focus should fall upon those above, who deemed him fit for purpose.

The fab four of Brailsford, Berrada, Ashworth and technical director Jason Wilcox now find themselves having to revisit the process of finding a man with the constitution to cope with a job that has spat out men of deeper talent than Ten Hag’s.

Far from introducing new methods and visionary thinking to the United project, the technical department has succeeded only in perpetuating muddle.

Indeed, apart from the savings made from the staff cull and cutting back of privileges, all of which have been wiped out by the compensation owed to Ten Hag, the involvement of Ineos has thus far delivered more of the same, and that’s a generous assessment.

Moreover the dithering and bad faith of the summer has seen the one outstanding candidate available, Tuchel, slip out of United’s grasp into the arms of another. The new broom sold itself as the solution to the puzzle of the post-Ferguson era. Instead it has become part of the problem. More Ine-loss than Ineos.
topics: Erik ten Hag, Manchester United FC, Premier League, Sir Dave Brailsford, Sports Comment, Subscribers

title: Man Utd line up Ruben Amorim to replace Erik ten Hag
body:
Amorim could be in charge for the Premier League clash with Chelsea

Manchester United are working on a deal to make Ruben Amorim their next manager, hours after Erik ten Hag was sacked.

Amorim, who until recently appeared content to stay at Sporting Lisbon – where he has enjoyed a blistering start to the season – will now be tasked with restoring this fallen giant to its former glories.

Rarely has a club been so well-prepared for replacing a sacked manager, given United chiefs have already spent months speaking to alternatives behind Ten Hag’s back.

After the Dutchman was handed his P45 by CEO Omar Berrada and sporting director Dan Ashworth in a meeting at the Carrington training base on Monday morning, the next appointment should happen quickly.

Ruud van Nistelrooy has been placed in temporary charge and will lead the side against Leicester City in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday night.

But sources have told i Amorim is someone well-liked by the United hierarchy, with a modern approach to the game that fits in with Ashworth and technical director Jason Wilcox’s ideal style of play.

The fact that United could usurp rivals Manchester City and snap up the Sporting Lisbon boss before he agrees to become Pep Guardiola’s long-term successor at the Etihad “only adds to the appeal”, one insider said.

Ineos had two major obstacles to bringing Amorim to Old Trafford. Amorim is not understood to be in any rush to leave Sporting, especially mid-season. The Portuguese champions have started the season in excellent form, winning 12 and drawing one of their 13 games thus far in all competitions.

Sacking Ten Hag is also understood to have cost United in the region of £15m and with Ineos undergoing vast cost-cutting exercises across the board, paying the substantial compensation fee Sporting will demand for Amorim is not a good look after making large numbers of staff redundant.

As a result, Van Nistelrooy is in charge at least on an interim basis. As i reported earlier this month, the former striker has been “acting like the boss” for a while, according to several sources.

Such was Van Nistelrooy’s growing visibility, Ten Hag snapped back, uncharacteristically, at questions over his new coaching staff before United’s 3-3 draw in Porto earlier this month, repeating the phrase “I appointed them myself”, clearly riled.

Van Nistelrooy went over to applaud United’s travelling supporters after the match, long after everyone else had made their way to the dressing room, as fans sang his name.

United and Sporting are understood to be working on reaching an agreement over compensation, understood to be in the region of €10m (£8.33m). If the two parties come to a swift conclusion, Amorim could be in place in time for the Premier League game against Chelsea on Sunday.

Amorim was lined up by Liverpool to be Jurgen Klopp’s successor at Anfield, but a clash of styles, with the young coach keen to instill a three-at-the-back system, a deal-breaker.

He also held talks over becoming David Moyes’s replacement at West Ham, before later apologising for the timing and publicity of the talks in London.

United’s new senior figures are more flexible than Liverpool were, sources said, as long as Amorim starts to instill “some form of identity” to their play – something Ten Hag was heavily criticised for not bringing to the table.

Given his remarkable achievements in Portugal – at the age of 36, Amorim led Sporting to a first league title in 19 years in 2021 and then won his second with the club last season – the Sporting boss was expected to follow sporting director Hugo Viana to City to become Guardiola’s successor.

Viana will replace Txiki Begiristain as City’s director of football next season and has a close relationship with Amorim at Sporting. United have moved fast as a result and look set to get one over on their big rivals.

Amorim may not have got a look in had Gareth Southgate not insisted he wants a break from coaching and Thomas Tuchel not been sworn in as the next England boss.

As i has previously reported, United’s hierarchy retain a long-standing interest in Southgate, even if the former England coach has never given any indication he wants the Old Trafford hotseat.
topics: Erik ten Hag, Gareth Southgate, Manchester United FC, Premier League, Sports News

title: Cristian Romero is becoming a problem for Tottenham
body:
The Argentine is a world-beater for his country but has made an error-strewn start to the season for his club

The decisive goal that Tottenham conceded at Selhurst Park on Sunday was the sort of collective calamity that makes supporters question why they even bother and causes managers to have sleepless nights.

Blame for Jean-Philippe Mateta’s winner for Crystal Palace can be apportioned to numerous individuals involved in the club’s fourth Premier League defeat of the season.

Guglielmo Vicario for playing the ball short despite making a dodgy start with his distribution; Cristian Romero for committing the cardinal sin of passing across his own box (compounded by it being looped horribly over to his central defensive colleague); Micky van de Ven for allowing the ball to run across his body, prompting Daniel Munoz to rush in and win possession; Pedro Porro and Romero (again) for dealing dismally with Munoz’s cross to the far post, allowing Mateta to score.

Finally, Ange Postecoglou for instructing his defenders to play this way against a team renowned for pressing high with intensity. Palace won 21 high turnovers, the second-most in a Premier League game this season. Maybe Pep Guardiola should take a share of the responsibility too for being so successful with this ploy that virtually every other manager in world football has since tried to copy him.

It was a nightmarish goal for Spurs to let in, an act of self-sabotage considering they had been fortunate to avoid conceding before they did with similarly sloppy play from their own six-yard box. No one player involved in it was any more or less at fault than anyone else; it was a collection of gaffes rather than one colossal cock-up.

However, as has been typical this season, Romero had a key part to play in it. According to the Premier League website, the Argentine hasn’t committed any errors leading to a goal this season. The bar must be set incredibly high given Romero has been at least partially culpable for over half of the 10 goals that Spurs have surrendered.

Romero can have no defence for three of them, all of which were strikingly similar. Against Leicester, Arsenal and Brighton, the 26-year-old was guilty of switching off and not staying close enough to his opposite man with Jamie Vardy, Gabriel Magalhaes and Danny Welbeck all profiting.

Those goals were consequential ones, either equalisers or winners that wiped four points off Tottenham’s tally.

Missteps against Newcastle and Palace were less clear but still costly. At St James’ Park, Romero embarked on an ambitious one-man press towards the halfway line and covered so much ground that he was unable to get back into position to prevent Harvey Barnes from flicking the Magpies in front.

When Alexander Isak added the crucial second from the middle of the penalty box, Romero was nowhere to be seen after pushing forward when the rest of the back four retreated.

Romero’s blooper reel is a combination of poor decision-making, sluggish ball-watching and needlessly risky passes. They are the sort of mistakes that he seldom makes for Argentina but often has for Spurs in the first few months of this season. Romero has been integral to a golden era of Argentine success, a defensive pillar in a team that has lifted the World Cup and back-to-back Copa Americas in the last three years.

He is consistently world-class when he pulls on the sky blue and white stripes. He is less commanding when he has the Tottenham cockerel on his chest; occasionally brilliant but often fallible.

There are plenty of potential explanations for that. Postecoglou’s high-risk strategy places an exceptional demand on central defenders, who are expected to be progressive in possession and proactive out of possession.

Romero has played virtually every game in three successive international tournaments in which his nation has reached a final.

Fifpro, the union for professional footballers worldwide, cited Romero in a study into player welfare, estimating that he covered over 162,000 kilometres of air travel in the 2023-24 season alone due to international commitments. That is bound to have drained him, mentally and physically.

Is his contractual situation a distraction? In June he will enter the final two years of his deal and rumours of Real Madrid interest continue to bubble away.

Despite his indifferent form, it seems unlikely Postecoglou will take him out of his team anytime soon. Romero has worn the armband in Son Heung-min’s injury-enforced absence and the Australian has spoken in glowing terms about his mentality and quality in the past.

He may point to a marked improvement in Romero’s disciplinary record – he is yet to receive a single card this season – as evidence of his burgeoning maturity.

Still, the more mistakes he makes, the less secure his place in the team should be. Other key players have paid the price for a slip in standards, James Maddison, subbed off at half-time and the hour mark in his last two games, chief among them. Democracy apparently underpins Postecoglou’s team selections. Radu Dragusin could be forgiven for thinking the rules don’t apply to him.

At his best, Romero is a titan of a centre-back and unquestionably one of Tottenham’s most important players, but at the moment his place in the side is based more on reputation than form. His lapses pose a problem for Postecoglou as he plots a way back from another disappointing defeat.
topics: Ange Postecoglou, Premier League, Sports Comment, Subscribers, Tottenham Hotspur FC

title: Celebrities will keep dying because of our obsession with youth
body:
There’s been one grim truth everyone keeps repeating since Liam Payne’s death: he was not the first, and he won’t be the last.

The circumstances change, but by now we can tell the story of the early death of a young celebrity by heart. It is no less tragic for its familiarity – the shock and grief, and even guilt, felt by the public in the days since the news broke has been an outpouring. We unanimously agree: fame was the killer. Had Payne never gone on The X Factor, had he never been in One Direction, he would have gone back to school, grown up, and lived beyond 31.

So how many more times does this nightmare have to play out before we reach a turning point and accept that teenagers, and certainly children (Payne was 14 when he first auditioned for The X Factor, 16 when he was successful), simply should not be famous at all? It is only a tiny minority who can really cope – and none of them come out unscathed.

If they’re lucky, a young star might have structure and reality imposed upon them from a responsible family and good management with their safety and best interests at heart. But that doesn’t change the fact that attention and recognition can do a lot of damage to a young person and warp their sense of self-worth.

Fame exposes you, it makes you vulnerable. It removes your innocence and sense of normality – it usually involves working around adults, often away from loved ones, when others the same age are sitting in a classroom. And while there are laws protecting child performers (and mandating their education), those only last until the end of the academic year they turn 16.

And all that’s when they’re still in the spotlight. The worst is usually yet to come. Nobody is responsible for the welfare of the “former” or “failed” once those 15 minutes are over and the applause has died out.

What is to be done then? I hear calls for better safeguarding, age limits, better duty of care, industry-wide regulation – all of it common sense, yet still very difficult to enforce in practice. Entertainment is the Wild West, it involves thousands of small projects spread across locations and countries and is financed by people with little interest in anything but more money, and populated with shady figures willing to mistreat the inexperienced.

What makes someone successful is unpredictable, what is considered “talent” is subjective. And so, so many people are driven to showbiz in a bid to change their fortunes. Desperation is easy to exploit.

But we will never stop making young people famous, because it would involve undoing something even more complex than the murky entertainment industry, a way of thinking that has dominated Western culture for centuries: we are obsessed with youth.

I’m not talking about preserving our youth, or chasing our youth. I am talking about our ingrained understanding that success of any kind is more impressive and more meaningful when it is achieved by the young. Until we stop rewarding precocity, everyone will continue racing toward recognition before time runs out.

Young people have always dominated the arts, from Mozart to Miley Cyrus, Judy Garland to Justin Bieber. However they end up in the spotlight – pushy parents, nepotism, reality TV, miracle, or pure hard graft – once they’re there we praise the confidence and self-possession that they display almost always with the phrase “beyond their years”. Look at Taylor Swift: in her 18-year recording career the most common consensus among critics trying to explain her success has been the sophistication with which she articulates her emotions, her ability to reflect on her life with a maturity beyond people double her age.

And of course, young achievement in any field patently is impressive – young politicians, student entrepreneurs. What makes artists different is that their early achievements turn them into products for our consumption.

Products need to be marketable to the biggest and most impressionable and aspirational possible audience: the young. So we present them with beautiful people they want to be, be friends with or fall in love with. We present them with singers and actors doing something extraordinary, so they can imagine they might do something extraordinary too. Young celebrities are expected to be role models for their child and teenage consumers – to be both relatable, and living out the fairy tale of their wildest dreams.

It doesn’t work the same way if someone becomes famous when they’re already an adult. We love to hear about late-career successes because it makes us think we, too, haven’t missed our chance to do something great, but we don’t marvel at their outsized talent as we might with a teenager who still has time to become a phenomenon, who still promises happiness, optimism, purity, energy, opportunity, vitality, naivete. Who has not learnt yet how hard life can be – or isn’t showing it.

We say we live in an age that values authenticity. I think that conceals the fact that we are still obsessed with youth and the young and will be until we stop fetishising the fantasy they represent and are ready to accept that life is difficult, ugly, and sad; until we celebrate hard work and failure that comes before success rather than deluding ourselves that it can happen overnight; until we can be patient and accept that greatness should take time. Time is not running out. It is much more likely to if fame comes too young.
topics: Celebrities, Liam Payne, The X Factor

title: Peaches: I went from 'brilliant feminist' to 'oversexed porn loser'
body:
When musician and performance artist Peaches released her turn-of-the-millennium breakthrough album Teaches of Peaches, she boldly stated she would not be moving towards the mainstream – she wanted the mainstream to come to her. It seemed an incredibly unlikely scenario.

Canadian-born Merrill Nisker was an entirely new type of pop star: unapologetically feminist, queer and sex positive; musically grimy and minimal; lyrically absurdist, funny and filthy, with a style that challenged gender norms.

Peaches would perform aggressively in a bra and ripped fishnets with unshaven armpits and fake pubic hair protruding from her crotch; the cover of Teaches of Peaches was a close-up photo of her crotch in pink hotpants.

Her signature tune was, and remains, 00’s “F**k the Pain Away”, a primitive eruption of harsh electronics and unrestrained sexual energy that contains an opening line for the ages: “Suckin’ on my titties like you wanted me/ Callin’ me all the time like Blondie/ Check out my Chrissie behind…”

And like all groundbreaking artists, Peaches had the shock of the new. She was an underground sensation for coming-of-age queer women, hip clubbers and fashionistas. “Some people were really having these crazy awakenings because they’d never realised they could express those things, or that it could be a possibility for them,” Nisker tells me over video call from her home in Berlin.

But that inevitably came with confusion and hostility elsewhere. A 2001 NME review after one of her first UK gigs – a showcase where she played before The Strokes – read, “Grandma, you’re scaring the kids”. She was 33 at the time.

This prompted Nisker to have an awakening of her own. “I was realising how polarising [my ideas] were to people. That’s the point that was shocking for me,” she says. “I was also realising how people would perceive me, how unaccepting people are, or how hungry they are for this, how the perception of me was so different – from ‘brilliant next wave feminist’ to ‘silly, dumb, oversexed porn loser’. I was way too angry or way too funny. Very old. I found out that I was ugly from the press. I was like, ‘Oh, I’m ugly.’ I mean, I didn’t think that I was ugly.”

And yet here in 2024, modern pop culture has adopted much of what Peaches stood for: female sexual liberation, queer identity, gender fluidity, rejection of the patriarchy, the right for women to express their messy, complicated selves. From Chappell Roan’s celebratory, searingly honest queer pop to Charli XCX’s Brat era via Cardi B’s sexually charged megahit “WAP” – CBC once called Peaches “the spiritual godmother of “WAP”” – the mainstream did actually move towards her. “Bizarre,” Nisker says. “I said it as a sort of cheeky statement to motivate myself, and also to separate myself from watered-down mainstream ideas. But it definitely came closer.”

Peaches’ role in the change should not be underestimated. She may not be a household name, but as a key, boundary-pushing cult figure, her influence has massively outsized her popularity. Madonna is a fan: it was said she worked out listening to Peaches and even invited Nisker to guest during the voguing catwalk segment of her Celebration tour in Berlin last year. And artists from Goldfrapp to Pink, Britney Spears to Christina Aguilera – who apparently played Peaches on repeat when writing her own sexual anthem “Dirrty” – all owe a debt. Even Radiohead were influenced, modelling their 2007 track “15 Step” on “F**k the Pain Away”. She duetted with Iggy Pop on 2003 album Fatherf**ker (where she wore an Abraham Lincoln-style beard on the cover), Yoko Ono was a fan and collaborator, and she was welcomed enthusiastically by the fashion community – “everyone in fashion digs Peaches” Vogue proclaimed as far as back as 2002.

Her music has become a staple on film and TV soundtracks, too, most famously as Bill Murray surveys a Japanese strip club to the sounds of “F**k the Pain Away” in Lost in Translation.

A new documentary, Teaches of Peaches, goes someway to explaining Neskir’s journey and influence. Produced by Judy Landkammer and Philipp Fussenegger, it doesn’t dwell too much on other aspects of her career – such as her 2010 one-woman DIY cabaret show Peaches Christ Superstar, or 2019 art exhibition Whose Jizz is This? – instead, taking Peaches’ 20th anniversary tour, Teaches of Peaches in 2022, as a jumping off point.

It gives a sense of her background – from a suburban Jewish family in Toronto – and her musical path: In the 90s, Nisker started out in a folk group called Mermaid Café before recasting herself in Berlin’s hedonistic counterculture with The Shit, an experimental electronic ensemble she formed with frequent collaborator, the Grammy-winner Chilly Gonzales (who provides the film with a gloriously louche presence). The film contains some intimate backstage shots and homemade footage, including some very sweet film of Neskir at her unlikely pre-stardom job teaching music to young children at YMCAs.

“I always thought, if there’s ever a documentary on me, that is going to be the moment that shocks people the most,” Nisker adds. But its centre point is the time-travel between Peaches initial rush and her recreation of Teaches of Peaches 20 years later. It is an interesting reflection on how a trailblazer relates to their work two decades on.

She says the nostalgic nature of the tour threw up some existential questions. “Like, what it meant for me: What is it? Is it relevant and interesting to play this music? How do I present it?” She came to “realise the power of my conceptual…ness. Not just the music, but the whole trying to bring to light these messages that were coded through humour and entertainment and a costume and pure performance.”

If anything, it was even more subversive: footage shows a then 55-year-old Peaches performing all-but-naked, save for some knickers. “I feel like because my body is older and different, I want to I show it even more,” she says. “It’s like, here it is!”

Peaches had to fight for her status. By the time she was 33 she had an ignored album under her own name, Fancypants Hoodlum, survived a brush with thyroid cancer and endured a significant break-up. But in Berlin she’d had an epiphany; she bought a Roland MC-505 groovebox, (a music production machine with in-built synthesisers, music sequencer and drum machine), changed her name to Peaches (after a line in a Nina Simone song) and began to make what was essentially a break-up album.

“I didn’t want to be a victim or sad, I was moving forward,” she says. “Not that I wasn’t grieving – and I do grieve. ‘Lovertits’ asks for forgiveness, but [the album] was a new exploration of what would be possible.”

German label Kitty-Yo singed Peaches, allowing her to go home to Toronto to make the album. There she lived with Leslie Feist – a fellow Canadian who would herself later enjoy Noughties pop success – and created the album in a haze of heartbreak and hedonism. Teaches of Peaches coincided with, and became a component of, the early Noughties electroclash movement headed by acts like Fischerspooner, Miss Kitten and Chicks on Speed – provocative, lo-fi, 80s-inspired electronics that straddled pop and artifice, its knowingly trashy aesthetics a precursor to what recently became known as “indie sleaze”.

When “F**k the Pain Away” blew up – “It blew up, but the label wouldn’t dare release it, right?” she interrupts – it wasn’t actually released as a single; the song was just a force of nature that couldn’t be held back. “And then years later, they were like, ‘Could you write something like ‘F**k the Pain Away’?’ So funny.” She’s still annoyed it wasn’t given an official release. “We’d had ‘I want to fuck you like an animal’ at the time, yeah? [In Nine Inch Nails’ “Closer”.] Which is a great song, but in terms of understanding attitudes…” she says, highlighting the double standards.

It wasn’t the only challenge she faced. People were confused by a solo performer whose only instrument onstage was a groovebox playing pre-recorded music. “People are used to that now, but back then it was unusual,” she says. “People were like is that a prop? Or was this fake? Was this real?” As a woman, she was continually underestimated – people didn’t believe she made her own music. “I mean it’s not that like they’re such amazingly technical beats or anything,” says Nisker.

There was one way she tried to anticipate reactions: by speaking, not singing, on the album. “That was calculated. With women, if you sing, all they do is talk about whether you’re a good singer, and the lyrics are secondary.” She just wishes she had today’s vocabulary to express herself. “In terms of language, in terms of understanding the queerness of it, the language wasn’t available then,” she says. “Or even the understanding of it. I was trying to figure it out.” Nisker therefore marvels at Chappell Roan. “[In the past, record labels] would have said, ‘You’ve got a great voice, but you could just change those lyrics?’” she says. “But it’s amazing. I don’t think we’ve ever seen somebody sing so outwardly, open, and uncoded about queer love in pop. Which is great. Also, Billie Eilish coming out. It’s a cute time in pop for queerness.”

She says, despite the strides forward for women and queer people, “there has been backlash in terms of safety, in terms of laws”. It’s why Peaches herself is even more outwardly feminist than ever; the film shows her performing in a pro-abortion shirt, for example. “Yeah, I think at the beginning I was more coding it,” she says. “But that was also how to bring people in. And now it’s just, if you know – let’s go.”

Teaches of Peaches is showing at the Doc’n Roll Film Festival
topics: Interviews, Music, Music Interviews

title: On TV tonight, Sophie Willan's Alma reunites with her rockstar dad
body:
Also, Ben Wheatley's zombie comedy Generation Z continues and Channel 5 goes behind the scenes at Broadmoor

10pm, BBC Two

Sophie Willan may be calling it a day with her Bafta-winning sitcom but she’s going out on an absolute high. This week’s episode expertly blends pathos and comedy as Alma (Willan) finally makes contact with the father who walked out on her mum Lin (Siobhan Finneran and those teeth!) when Alma was a baby. Grandmother Joan (the mighty Lorraine Ashbourne) recalls that this rock-star wannabe was “tall, thin and walked like a moody gorilla”, while Alma herself was convinced that he was really Richard Ashcroft of The Verve. Disappointment surely beckons as Craig Parkinson (Line Of Duty, Grace) guests.

8pm, BBC One

A second chance to do what, you might ask? To destroy American democracy while ensuring he stays out of prison and throws Ukraine to the Russian wolves? In any case, as we stand Donald Trump has an even chance of returning to the White House in November, and this is Panorama’s take on the convicted felon’s election campaign.

9pm, BBC One

Miraculously, Bernardine Evaristo’s novel doesn’t feel too overstretched by this eight-part adaptation, the inter-generational aspect given space to breathe. The focus in the opening episode of this double-bill is mostly on Barry’s daughters Donna and Maxine (Sharlene Whyte and Tamara Lawrence).

9pm, BBC Two

Professor Brian Cox shares his wonderment at the solar system’s frozen places, revealing the dwarf planet where mountains of solid ice float across the surface and the black and white moon painted with frost.

9pm, Channel 4

The zombie pensioners are on the rampage and the authorities are trying to hush it up with a spot of fake news blaming it all on foot-and-mouth disease. Ben Wheatley’s ongoing satire on inter-generational tensions (kind of Skins meets Shaun Of The Dead) isn’t exactly subtle but it is fun, as Kelly (Buket Komur) battles with her conflicting feelings about having to kill her rampaging nan, while Morgan (Robert Lindsay) begins some private sleuthing into the causes of the outbreak.

10pm, Channel 4

The docuseries about cruel romance fraudsters continues with the case of an American woman who claimed to have MS and conned her partner into running up huge debts to fund her “treatment” (read lifestyle) before falsely accusing him of domestic violence. When she threatened to kill herself in Japan unless friends raised $20,000 that she claimed had been stolen, people started to question the truth of her stories and the FBI became involved.

10pm, Channel 5

It took a long while for the psychiatric hospital to allow cameras into their high-security confines, but they never seem to leave now. This is the latest docuseries (ITV began the process back in 2014), which here looks at how staff deal with violent inmates: Lee Rigby’s killer Michael Adebowale assaulting a nurse at Broadmoor, and the attack on Peter Sutcliffe that left the Yorkshire Ripper blind in one eye.
topics: TV Guide

title: I can’t open my mouth without my teenage daughters cancelling me - I’m exhausted
body:
Gen Z’s zero tolerance policies are a nightmare for parents – although that doesn’t mean they’re not right, says Laura Craik

Any parent of teens will tell you that dinner time can be a fraught affair. Whoever cooks the meals in your family can count themselves blessed if their teenager hasn’t gone vegetarian, vegan, wheat-free, carb-free or low-GI by the time they’ve turned 15. But however restrictive their diet, it’s nowhere near as restrictive as the conversation topics that you, their clueless, hapless parent, will rapidly find yourself adhering to as you tensely break (gluten-free) bread around the kitchen table.

Whoever said “the family that eats together, stays together” clearly wasn’t a parent in 2024. If they had been, they’d likely have found themselves cancelled for daring to utter such an insensitive statement. What’s insensitive about it? I’ve absolutely no idea – but your teen will find one. How dare you manipulate them into eating dinner with you by suggesting that if they don’t, they’re not a team player? What if they don’t want to eat? Are you trying to fat shame them? And so on.

Cancel culture runs rife in every arena, from the boardroom to the classroom to X. But there’s a particularly deep wound derived from being cancelled by your own kids, in your own home – one of the only spaces left where you feel able to speak freely.

“Someone’s having a fag,” I once said, sniffing the air like the bloodhound I am, an olfactory superpower which has so far acted as an effective deterrent against either of my daughters taking up smoking.

“MUM!” shouted my then-13 year-old, so unexpectedly that I dropped my forkful of meat-free, taste-free, joy-free escalope. “YOU CAN’T SAY THAT!”

Truly, I didn’t know. In the 1990s, it’s just what everyone called their Marlboro Lights. In the 1960s and 1970s, it was another word for ‘boring’. You had to tidy your room? What a fag. At Eton, it was used to describe young boys who did errands for older boys, but maybe best not to dwell on that one. Anyway, I was assured I absolutely couldn’t, shouldn’t, mustn’t describe a cigarette in this way again.

The latest high-profile instance of mother-daughter cancelling comes courtesy of Lyla Elichaoff, 21, and Esme Bertelsen, 23, who are on the cover of this month’s Tatler on account of being the respective offspring of Trinny Woodall and Susannah Constantine.

This fearsome duo’s seminal yet controversial TV makeover show, What Not to Wear, was hugely popular throughout the early 2000s, peaking at 4.92 million viewers and making its presenters household names. Have the daughters who so benefit from their mothers’ success actually bothered watching the show? Nah. But they still have opinions. “I think they would be cancelled if the show was made now,” Trinny’s daughter, Lila, told Tatler. “You can’t really speak to people like that any more, and say things like, ‘You’re so ugly’.”

Lila has a point. Trinny and Susannah did indeed say some dubious things to their guests, calling out their “saddlebags” or “lack of tits”. We were all more cavalier and hurtful in the early aughts, and it’s one of the very best things about Gen Z that they strive to be more respectful of each other’s bodies, and mindful of how they talk about them.

All parents should learn from this. Any parent who body shames their child should not only be cancelled, but informed of the lasting harm it can do to a child’s self esteem. As with their zero tolerance policy towards racism and sexism, Gen Z’s stance against sizeism is absolutely right.

And stringent policing, censoring and criticising of mum and dad’s opinions is a natural part of evolution. Teens wouldn’t be teens if they weren’t rejecting their parents’ POV: it’s partly how they learn to define themselves.

It’s just that sometimes, so vast is the list of cancellable topics that an innocent five-minute dinner time convo can leave you feeling like the lovechild of Elon Musk and Jeffree Star. You put avocado in the salad? You’re cancelled (air miles). You bought something from Primark? You’re cancelled (fast fashion). You called Tilly “Tilly” when they want to be known as Travis, even though nobody told you? So cancelled.

One mum of my acquaintance was even cancelled for daring to suggest her daughter put on a cardigan before leaving the house. “Are you slut shaming me?” asked her 15 year-old. No: merely worried that her daughter would be cold.

As a teen, I remember biting my tongue when my mother said something insensitive. “She’s of a different generation,” I’d think. Only the most egregious comments would elicit a telling off, but even then I’d pick my words. “We don’t say that now,” I’d explain. “It’s culturally insensitive, because….” The explanation was essential, since it sought to educate rather than simply argue for the sake of it.

By contrast, my own teens (and the teens of most of my friends, though they would also concede that girls are ‘worse’ than boys, if such a sentiment dare be expressed) are quicker to be outraged and faster to condemn.

One of our worst family arguments arose from me bitching – quite mildly – about the French. Apparently, you can’t say that Parisians are rude. You can’t even say that you find them rude based on your own experience of working in Paris four times a year for the past 20 years. “But they once served me partially frozen chicken when I was six months pregnant then swore at me when I asked them to reheat it,” I wailed. But that’s another thing that’s verboten: daring to complain about restaurant service or food.

For some teens, the cancellation list is long, but surprisingly flexible – and never more so than when it comes to style. Victoria’s Secret might have sketchy links to Jeffrey Epstein, but they’ll still stay up late to watch its fashion show. Brandy Melville might be questionable for its sizing policy, except when they do a really cute top.

Maybe we’re all hypocrites in the end, cherry-picking our causes. If your teens criticise your views, consider it a learning opportunity. Remember that they’re growing up in a time when there’s no margin for error: everything they say or write can be documented online, where it will remain for all eternity. No wonder their moral compass is so finely attuned.

Better that they’re idealistic and thoughtful than cynical and tactless. And better that they correct you than let you go forth into the world inadvertently causing offence.

title: Love salmon for dinner? You might not after you read this
body:
It’s delicious, nutritious and versatile – but increasingly one of the most controversial foods you can put on your plate, finds Clare Finney

Revered for centuries as the king of fishes, in more recent years Atlantic salmon has become better known as the battery chicken of the sea. The culprit? Salmon farms: once a cottage industry, confined to a few wooden pens run by Scottish crofters, now the country’s fastest growing food production business, responsible for £580m of trade in 2023 alone.

Nearly 30 per cent of all fish consumed in the UK is farmed salmon, and we’re not alone in our appreciation: Scottish salmon is the country’s top food export globally. Yet as with any animal protein, with great demand comes great challenges around ethics and sustainability, and as chefs and consumers have become ever more interested in where their food comes from, the issues have become more pressing.

The problem – as salmon farming’s critics see it – is one of scale. In 1980, Scottish farmers landed 600 tonnes of salmon; by 2023, this had reached 187,725 tonnes. Ireland’s production pales into comparison – around 15,000 tonnes annually – but has still grown exponentially in the past 30 years. In both countries, salmon is farmed in “open” pens – a method of farming outlawed in several countries, but has so far had free rein in the UK.

Anyone who has flown over the west coasts of Scotland and Ireland may well have spotted the ring-shaped pens along sea lochs and shorelines. At first glance, they seem unobtrusive; yet beneath the surface lies a different story.

Every one of these pens will hold between 30,000 to one million adult fish in open nets that allow water in, but also allow the flow of waste, sea lice and chemicals used to treat the lice, out into the surrounding environment with occasionally disastrous consequences.

“Any large-scale food production comes with an environmental impact. It doesn’t matter whether it’s broad beans, cows, chickens or salmon,” says Adam Hughes, a marine ecologist and Professor of Innovation in the so-called “Blue Economy” (the term for the economic activities associated with the oceans and seas).

In the case of salmon, these impacts include faecal matter and uneaten food deposited beneath the pens, sea lice and chemicals used to treat sea lice. “It is carefully monitored by salmon farms, and limits are set by regulatory agencies but the natural environment is relied upon to accumulate that waste,” says Hughes – which, if you think about it, “is no different to terrestrial farming.”

Yet the impacts of terrestrial farming are more readily felt and seen. What consumers haven’t realised – up until relatively recently – is the extent to which the waste produced by salmon farming is affecting not just the surrounding environment, but the salmon themselves.

Lice might sound innocuous, but in fact, they cause huge welfare issues for farmed salmon, effectively eating the fish alive. En masse, lice can kill a fish, and salmon farms are all about mass. In such crowded pens, lice spread as effectively – but far more lethally – as head lice do in schools. The mortality rate in itself is cause for alarm – in February this year, the Fish Health Inspectorate revealed that mortalities on Scottish salmon farms reached 17.4 million in 2023, exceeding those the year before.

But it’s the impact of salmon farming on wild salmon and other species that are a particular source of controversy. As the number of farmed salmon has risen exponentially in the past 50 years, wild salmon populations have dwindled to the point where even seeing one, let alone catching one, is a rarity.

Where once the leaping of wild salmon up the river to their birthplace to breed was a highlight of the Scottish culinary calendar, with fish so numerous that locals could feast for weeks, now many rivers have catch and release policies, or limit the number of salmon that can be kept.

There are even heavier restrictions in England and Wales, where it is illegal to sell salmon caught in the wild. Just last week, figures from the Environment Agency and Cefas showed the number of wild Atlantic salmon caught by rod and line in England and Wales had dropped to a record low – down to 5,399 when as recently as 2017 it was 20,000.

In September, an annual salmon count recorded the lowest ever number of juveniles – that is, young salmon heading out to sea – in Frome, one of the country’s most important rivers for the species. In Ireland, where wild salmon can – with strict regulation – be caught to sell for consumption, wild salmon numbers have declined by almost 80 per cent in the past 20 years.

Admittedly the causes are complex, and by no means confined to salmon farms. “The Scottish Government has identified 13 high-level pressures and more than 40 specific pressures facing wild salmon – and the main issues in Scotland are water quality (sewage and agricultural pollution) and habitat loss,” says Salmon Scotland, the trade body representing Scotland’s salmon industry. It argues that decline in wild salmon numbers has been recorded across the globe, “including on the east coast of Scotland, England and across Europe, where there have never been any salmon farms.”

Indeed, scientists investigating the situation in Frome cited sewage and agricultural run-off as key factors. Other causes cited by the International Union for Conservation of Nature include climate change, which reduces the availability of prey, as well as dams and other barriers in the rivers blocking access to spawning and feeding grounds.

Yet the life cycle of a wild salmon remains so poorly understood, it’s impossible to rule salmon farms out as a factor – especially given their proximity to wild salmon’s migratory routes. From their birthplace in the riverbed to their feeding grounds in Greenland and back again, during their lifetime salmon travel over 2000 miles, through saline water and fresh – and no one knows how they navigate. Regardless of where you stand on farmed salmon, it is extraordinary that humans can even try to simulate this trajectory artificially and at scale.

It is also hard to believe there aren’t consequences for the wild fish. Most farmed salmon are from a limited gene pool and have been selectively bred for growth rate, disease resistance and age of maturation; traits which are profitable for salmon farmers, but disastrous for the few wild Atlantic salmon left in our waters. Both storms and seals have been known to rip holes in the pens, permitting farmed fish to escape; as recently as August, thousands of farmed salmon escaped in Connemara, western Ireland, and were subsequently found in the rivers in which wild Atlantic salmon swim and spawn.

Nor is it just wild salmon that are suffering. Though most livestock farms are working to decrease their dependence on chemicals, the salmon farming industry has done the reverse in its bid to cope with soaring mortality rates. Excessive antibiotic usage is feared to increase antimicrobial resistance among humans, but “salmon farms are the only livestock industry to have increased their antibiotic usage in recent years” says Matt Palmer, once a veterinary surgeon on an intensive Scottish salmon farm, now Campaign Manager at Wild Fish; a conservation charity dedicated to reversing the decline in wild fish populations. Meanwhile, pesticides, also used to combat disease, seep into the surrounding water and can affect crustaceans up to 40km (25 miles) away.

Organic farmed salmon, although stocking density is lower, natural sea lice control methods are used and antibiotics only under authorised control, are not immune from contamination either. “It’s just a net in the sea. However minimal the farm is, there is no way that by-products and lice [from non-organic farms] don’t get into the surrounding area,” says Ed Smith; a food writer and one of a growing number of high-profile chefs to have sworn off salmon in recent years in an effort to highlight the issues around farming.

In fact, the last straw for Smith was not the lice, escapees or chemical pollution – all of which the Scottish Environment Agency has made concerted efforts to improve in recent years. “A lot is being done to reduce lice numbers, and the amount of medicines which farms are allowed to release has been reduced greatly,” says Hughes. Antibiotic use has plummeted, new pens must meet strict criteria to limit escapees and build-up of organic matter, and freshwater baths or symbiotic cleaner fish like wrasse are being used to combat lice, instead of harsh chemicals.

Yet no farm or government agency has yet been able to address the biggest barrier to long-term sustainability, which is the amount of wild fish that must be caught and killed to feed the farmed salmon. The Foraged (Wild) Fish Dependency Ratio (FFDR) is used to measure the amount of wild fish ingredients in the feed, and their yield ratio. On average, the global ratio for farmed salmon is 1.5 – meaning more fish are killed to feed the salmon than salmon is yielded to feed humans. “That crystallised the problem, for me,” Smith says.

“They [salmon] are apex predators, at the top of the food chain. To catch fish like mackerel, wild herring and anchovies – fish that humans can [and do] eat – to produce salmon is a totally inefficient way of farming and eating,” he continues. Substituting a proportion of this with plants – as many organic salmon farms do – hasn’t helped much, because of the environmental cost of growing, transporting and processing the plants into something that offers the nutrients required for a carnivorous species.

There is one company, though, that may have found a way past this seemingly insurmountable hurdle. Loch Duart, which sells via the online fish market Pesky Fish describes its salmon as “the very first farmed salmon that we can qualify as regenerative”, according to Pesky Fish’s founder, Ben King. “The term regenerative is overused, but we judge against three criteria, no matter what the species.”

Loch Duart has reduced its dependency on wild stocks by sourcing its marine content from industry trimmings from MSC certified fisheries. “There is such large volume in fish processing, so there is a huge amount of by-product potentially going to landfill,” he explains. “Using that to feed fish reduces dependence on wild-caught fish.”

King says they have also engaged with local fishing associations to measure stock levels of existing species and marine vegetation around the farm to ensure no signs of degradation.

“One of the ways we gauge the effect of a farm on the surrounding environment is by taking a bit of the seabed underneath the pen and measuring its contents. Conventional salmon farms have to keep moving the pens because they are destroying the seabed beneath. It is dead, not thriving. But Loch Duart is not seeing the same effects.”

Loch Duart is “not perfect,” King concedes. The ethical and environmental implications of sourcing and transporting wrasse to salmon farms is still a bone of contention, as are Loch Duart’s methods of deterring the seals who are constantly finding new ways to break into the pens. Yet “in a murky environment, they are a single beacon” – and striving to improve.

There are others. In Iceland, salmon is now being reared on closed net farms on land, in a controlled environment – a model that may be tricky to replicate sustainably in the UK (though there are plans to try it in Yorkshire) but works well in Iceland, where there is more land, and abundant renewable energy. In Norway, Hughes mentions “technologies being developed where salmon cages are almost fully enclosed; still in the sea but enclosed to the extent that issues around lice and waste material are negated. They are being trialled in Norway, and companies want to bring them into Scotland,” he explains.

So what can we as consumers do in the meantime? Buying Loch Duart seems an obvious choice, but it’s an expensive one. “It’s much more expensive than the local supermarket,” says Harry Lobek, director of London Shell Co fishmonger and restaurant in north London. “Fish isn’t something people should be scrimping on, and the correlation is generally that the higher the quality the higher the price,” he continues – but if £6 a fillet [the Loch Duart price] makes your eyes water, there are more, cheaper fish in the sea. “Gurnard, grey mullet, Whiting, megrim sole etc… I would prefer to sell over salmon. They are cheaper too. But sadly they aren’t as popular and seem to be more of a connoisseur’s choice,” continues Lobek.

There’s too much money at stake for salmon farming not to up its game – and between farming fish and farming meat, the former remains the least carbon-intensive option. “There are definitely ways in which the industry can become more sustainable,” says Hughes, “but it will come at a cost, and someone has to pick up that cost.”

If we want our salmon farms to transition toward a more sustainable way of operating, we must accept paying more for a product which, up to this point, has come cheap at the expense of our sea.
